blocks.html: 6 Applications of the trace formula to trigonometric sums
Applications to trigonometric sums
In this exposé, I explain how the trace formula makes it possible to compute or study various trigonometric sums, and how, combined with the Weil conjecture, it can make it possible to bound them.

The first two sections give a “user's guide” to these tools. Section 3 is an account, in cohomological language, of Weil's results on sums in \(1\) variable. Sections \(4\) to \(6\) form a detailed study of Gauss and Jacobi sums — including Weil's old and recent results on the Hecke characters defined by Jacobi sums. In section \(7\), we study a several-variable generalization of Kloosterman sums. Finally, in section \(8\), one will find some indications on other uses that have been made or can be made of these methods.
6 Notations

We use the notations of [II]Rapport, section 1. We shall often have to consider a finite extension \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\subset \mathbb{F}\) of \(\mathbb{F}_q\). We shall denote by a subscript \(0\) an object over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and by a subscript \(1\) an object over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\). Replacing a subscript \(0\) by a subscript \(1\) (resp. suppressing the subscript) means that one extends the scalars to \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\) (resp. to \(\mathbb{F}\)).

We denote by \(\ell\) a prime number \(\ne p\). We freely use the language of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves, as well as that of \(E_\lambda\)-sheaves, for \(E_\lambda\) a finite extension of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) (cf. [II]Rapport, section 2 and especially 2.11).
Let \(H^\bullet\) be a graded vector space. If \(T\) is an endomorphism of \(H^\bullet\), we set (cf. [IV]Cycle, 1.3.5)
\[ \operatorname{tr}(T,H^\bullet) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(T,H^i) \text{.} \]
1 Principles

Let \(X_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(E_\lambda\) a finite extension of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X-0\). The trace formula says that
\[ \tag{1.1.1} \sum_{x\in X^F} \operatorname{tr}(F_x^\ast,\mathscr{F}) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\right) \text{.} \]
With the notation 0.3, the right-hand side is written simply \(\operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F}))\).

This trace formula for \(E_\lambda\)-sheaves can either be deduced from [II]Rapport 4.10 by passage to the limit (cf. [II]Rapport 4.11 to 4.13), or be deduced from the trace formula for \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves ([II]Rapport 3.2) by the method of ([III]Fonctions \(L\) mod. \(\ell^n\), 4.3).
We are going to interpret various trigonometric sums as the left-hand side of (1.1.1), for suitable \(X_0\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\).

Let \(A\) be a finite group. An \(A\)-torsor on a scheme \(X\) is a sheaf \(T\) on \(X\), equipped with a right action of \(A\), which, locally (for the étale topology) on \(X\), is isomorphic to the constant sheaf \(A\) on which \(A\) acts by right translation.

If \(\tau:A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} B\) is a homomorphism, and \(T\) an \(A\)-torsor, there exists, up to unique isomorphism, one and only one \(B\)-torsor \(\tau(T)\), equipped with a morphism of sheaves \(\tau:T\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \tau(T)\) such that
\[ \tag{1.2.1} \tau(t a) = \tau(t) \tau(a)\text{.} \]

If \(T\) is an \(A\)-torsor on \(X\), and \(\rho\) a linear representation of \(A\): \(\rho:A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{gl}(V)\) (\(V\) a finite-dimensional vector space over \(E_\lambda\)), there exists, up to unique isomorphism, a unique \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\), smooth of rank \(\dim(V)\), equipped with a morphism of sheaves
\[ \tag{1.2.2} \rho:T\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{Isom}}(V,\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

such that \(\rho(t a) = \rho(t) \rho(a)\). We denote it by \(\rho(T)\). For \(\tau:A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} B\) and \(\rho\) a representation of \(B\), we have a canonical isomorphism \(\rho(\tau(T)) = (\rho\tau)(T)\).

In this section (except for the appendix), we consider only the case where \(A\) is commutative and where \(V=E_\lambda\): \(\rho\) is a character \(A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\), and \(\rho(T)\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf smooth of rank one. The morphism (1.2.2) is interpreted as an everywhere nonzero morphism
\[ \tag{1.2.3} \rho:T\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \rho(T) \]
such that \(\rho(t a) = \rho(a)\rho(t)\).
Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a commutative group scheme over \(S\), and \(G'\) an extension of commutative group schemes over \(S\)
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & A \ar[r] & G' \ar[r]^-\pi & G \ar[r] & 0 . } \]
The sheaf \(T\) of local sections of \(\pi\) is then an \(A\)-torsor on \(G\).
If \(X\) is a scheme over \(S\), and \(f,g\) two \(S\)-morphisms from \(X\) to \(G\), then, owing to the fact that \(T\) is defined by an extension, we have a canonical isomorphism
\[ \tag{1.3.1} (f+g)^\ast T = f^\ast T + g^\ast T \text{.} \]
On the left, \(f+g\) is the sum of \(f\) and \(g\), in the sense of the group law of \(G\); on the right, \(+\) denotes a sum of torsors.

If \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G\) factors through \(G'\), then \(f^\ast T\) is trivial (and a factorization gives a trivialization); up to (non-unique) isomorphism, the \(A\)-torsor \(f^\ast T\) depends only on the image of \(f\) in \(\hom_S(X,G)/\pi\hom_S(X,G')\): it is given by the morphism \(\partial\) in the exact sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ \hom(X,G') \ar[r] & \hom(X,G) \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,A) . } \]

We shall apply these constructions to the Kummer exact sequences \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\), and to the Lang torsors.
1.4 The Lang torsor
Let \(G_0\) be a connected commutative algebraic group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) (for the non-commutative case, see the appendix). The group law is written multiplicatively. The Lang isogeny
\[ \mathfrak{L}:G_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_0: x\mapsto F x\cdot x^{-1} \]

is étale; its image, an open subgroup of \(G_0\), can only be \(G_0\) itself; its kernel is the finite group \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\). The Lang torsor \(L\) is the \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\)-torsor on \(G_0\) defined by the exact sequence
\[ \tag{1.4.1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & G_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \ar[r] & G_0 \ar[r]^-{\mathfrak{L}} & G_0 \ar[r] & 0 . } \]
Notation

We again denote by \(L\) and \(\mathfrak{L}\) (or \(L_{(q)}\) and \(\mathfrak{L}_{(q)}\)) the objects deduced from \(L\) and \(\mathfrak{L}\) by extension of the base field. If need be, one will specify by a subscript \(0\) or \(1\).
Examples
For \(G_0=\mathbb{G}_a\) or \(\mathbb{G}_m\), the sequences (1.4.1) are written

\begin{align*} \tag{1.4.2} &\xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathbb{F}_q \ar[r] & \mathbb{G}_a \ar[r]^-{x^q-x} & \mathbb{G}_a \ar[r] & 0 } \\ \tag{1.4.3} &\xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \boldsymbol{\mu}_{q-1} \ar[r] & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r]^-{x^{q-1}} & \mathbb{G}_m \ar[r] & 0 } \end{align*}

Let us compute the endomorphism \(F^\ast\) of the fibre of the Lang torsor at \(\gamma\in G^F=G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\). If \(g\in \mathfrak{L}^{-1}(\gamma)\subset G\), then \(F g = F g\cdot g^{-1}\cdot g = \gamma g\). Consequently ([II]Rapport, 1.2)
\[ \tag{1.5.1} \text{on } L_0(G_0)_\gamma\simeq \mathfrak{L}^{-1}(\gamma) \text{, } F^\ast \text{ is } g\mapsto g\gamma^{-1} \text{.} \]

Over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\), the identity \(F_{(q^n)}=F_{(q)}^n\) between endomorphisms of \(G_1\) implies that \(\mathfrak{L}_{(q^n)}=\mathfrak{L}_{(q)}\circ \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} F_{(q)}^i\). On \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})\), \(F_{(q)}^i\) acts as the element \(x\mapsto x^{q^i}\) of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q)\). On \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})\), \(\prod F_{(q)}^i\) is therefore the composite of the norm \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\) and the inclusion \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\subset G_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})\): the diagram

\[ \tag{1.6.1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & G_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}) \ar[r] \ar[d]^-N & G_1 \ar[r]^-{\mathfrak{L}_{(q^n)}} \ar[d]^-{\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} F_{(q)}^i} & G_1 \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & G_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \ar[r] & G_q \ar[r]^-{\mathfrak{L}_{(q)}} & G_1 \ar[r] & 0 } \]
is commutative. In the language of torsors, this yields an isomorphism canonical between \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\)-torsors on \(G_1\)
\[ \tag{1.6.2} N L_{(q^n)} = L_{(q)} \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.7

Let \(f_0:X_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_0\) be a morphism and \(\chi:G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\) a character. We set \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0) = \chi^{-1}(f_0^\ast (L_0(G_0))) = f_0^\ast\chi^{-1}(L_0(G_0))\).
We have the following functoriality properties:

1. \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)\) is bimultiplicative in \(\chi\) and \(f_0\):

    \begin{align*} \tag{1.7.1} \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0'\cdot f_0'') &= \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0')\otimes \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0'') \text{,} \\ \tag{1.7.2} \mathscr{F}(\chi'\chi'',\mathscr{F}_0) &= \mathscr{F}(\chi',f_0)\otimes \mathscr{F}(\chi'',f_0) \text{.} \end{align*}

    This follows from the definition of \(\chi(T)\), for \(T\) a torsor, together with (1.3.1) for (1.7.1).

  2. For \(g_0:Y_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_0\) a morphism, we have

    \[ \tag{1.7.3} \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0\circ g_0) = g_0^\ast \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0) \text{.} \]

    In particular, \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0) = f_0^\ast \mathscr{F}(\chi)\), where \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\) denotes \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,\operatorname{id}_{G_0})\),

  3. For \(u_0:G_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} H_0\) a morphism, and \(\chi:H_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\), we have

    \[ \tag{1.7.4} \mathscr{F}(\chi,u_0 f_0) = \mathscr{F}(\chi u_0,f_0) \text{.} \]

  4. For \(G_0=\prod_{i\in I} G_0^i\), \(\chi\) with coordinates \(\chi_i\) (\(i\in I\)) and \(f_0\) with coordinates \(f_0^i\), it follows from (1.7.1) to (1.7.4) that

    \[ \tag{1.7.5} \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0) = \bigotimes_{i\in I} \mathscr{F}(\chi_i,f_0^i) \text{.} \]
Note the \(\chi^{-1}\) in Definition 1.7. It ensures that, for \(x\in X^F\), one has on \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)_x\)
\[ \tag{1.7.6} F_x^\ast = \chi f_0(x) \]
(use that the fibre at \(x\) of the morphism (1.2.2), for \(\rho=\chi^{-1}\), commutes with \(F_x^\ast\), and (1.5.1)).
If \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)_1\) is the sheaf deduced from \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)\) by extension of the base field to \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\), we deduce from (1.6.2) that
\[ \tag{1.7.7} \mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)_1 = \mathscr{F}(\chi\circ N,f_1) \text{.} \]
1.8 Abuse of notation

(i) If \(\Xi\) is a notation for the composite map \(\chi f_0:X_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\), we shall sometimes write \(\mathscr{F}(\Xi)\) instead of \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)\). Thanks to (1.7.1) to (1.7.5), there is hardly any risk of ambiguity. For example:

1. one writes \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\) for \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,\operatorname{id}_{G_0})\) (notation already used in 1.7b));

  2. one writes \(\mathscr{F}(\chi f_0)\) for \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)\);

  3. with the notations of 1.7d), one writes \(\mathscr{F}(\prod \chi_i f_0^i)\) for \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f))\).

With this notation, (1.7.4) expresses that the expression \(\mathscr{F}(\chi u_0 f_0)\) is not ambiguous, (1.7.1) (1.7.2) (1.7.5) express a multiplicativity of \(\mathscr{F}(\Xi)\) in \(\Xi\), and (1.7.6) is rewritten \(F_x^\ast = \Xi(x)\) on \(\mathscr{F}(\Xi)_x\).

(ii) If \(X\) is a scheme over an extension \(k\) of \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(f\) is a morphism from \(X\) to \(G_0\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q} k\), we shall again denote by \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f)\), \(\mathscr{F}(\chi f)\), or \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\) (for \(f\) an inclusion) the inverse image by \(f\) of the \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf deduced from \(\chi^{-1}(L_0(G))\) by extension of the scalars from \(\mathbb{F}_q\) to \(k\). If \(f_0\) is the composite \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_0\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q} k \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_0\), it is again the \(\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0)\) of 1.7. For \(k\) a finite extension of \(\mathbb{F}_q\), we have \(\mathscr{F}(\chi f) = \chi(\chi N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q} f)\).
Applying (1.1.1) to (1.7.6) and (1.7.7), we find:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.9

Let \(S_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(G_0\) a connected commutative algebraic group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(f_0:S_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_0\) a morphism and \(\chi:G_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\). We have

\[ \tag{1.9.1} \sum_{s\in S_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \chi f_0(s) = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(S,\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0))) \]

and, for every integer \(n\geqslant 1\)

\[ \tag{1.9.2} \sum_{s\in S_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})} \chi\circ N_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q} f_0(s) = \operatorname{tr}({F^\ast}^n, \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet\left(S,\mathscr{F}(\chi,f_0))\right) \text{.} \]
Take for \(G_0\) a product. With the notations of 1.7d) and 1.8c), formula (1.9.2) becomes

\[ \sum_{s\in S_0(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})} \prod_i \chi_i\circ N_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q} (f_0^i(s)) = \operatorname{tr}\Big({F^\ast}^n, \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet\Big(S,\mathscr{F}\Big(\prod_i \chi_i f_0^i\Big)\Big)\Big) \text{.} \]
Take \(G_0=\{e\}\). Formula (1.9.1) becomes
\[ \left|S_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\right| = \sum_{s\in S_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} 1 = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(S,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)) \text{.} \]
It is rare that one can explicitly compute the right-hand side of (1.9.1). Here is an amusing example, with \(G_0=\{e\}\).
1.10 Example
A non-singular projective quadric of odd dimension over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) has the same number of rational points as the projective space over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) of the same dimension.

If, over \(\mathbb{C}\), \(X\) is a non-singular quadric hypersurface in the projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{2 N}\), and \(Y\) a hyperplane, it is known that for \(i\leqslant 2\dim(X)=2\dim(Y)\), the inclusions \(X\hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{2 N}\hookleftarrow Y\) induce isomorphisms (in ordinary cohomology)
\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Q}) & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathbb{P}^{2 N},\mathbb{Q}) \ar[r]^-\sim \ar[l]_-\sim& \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(Y,\mathbb{Q}) . } \]

By specialization, it follows that if \(X_0'\) is a non-singular quadric hypersurface in the projective space \(\mathbb{P}_0^{2 N}\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(Y_0'\) a hyperplane, the inclusions \(X_0'\hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}_0^{2 N}\hookleftarrow Y_0'\) induce isomorphisms

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X',\mathbb{Q}_\ell) & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathbb{P}^{2 N},\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \ar[r]^-\sim \ar[l]_-\sim& \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(Y',\mathbb{Q}_\ell) . } \]
These isomorphisms commute with \(F^\ast\), and we apply the trace formula.

One can also use the trace formula to understand the classical formulas giving the number of rational points of the linear groups over the finite fields, and those of certain homogeneous spaces (see section 8).

We have at our disposal a dictionary allowing us to translate into cohomological terms various types of classical manipulations on trigonometric sums. This dictionary will be given in section 2. Since the cohomological statement is more “geometric,” it can sometimes apply to situations where the classical argument applies only after an extension of the base finite field. Here is an example (a special case of a theorem of Kazhdan).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.13 (Kazhdan)

Let \(X_0\) be a scheme over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). Suppose that there exists an action \(\rho\) of \(\mathbb{G}_a\) on \(X\), and a morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) of schemes over \(\mathbb{F}\), making \(X\) a \(\mathbb{G}_a\)-torsor on \(Y\). Then the number of rational points of \(X_0\) is divisible by \(q\).
Suppose first that \(\rho\), \(Y\) and \(f\) are defined over \(\mathbb{F}_q\).
Classical argument

The fibres of \(f:X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\) all have \(q\) elements: \(|X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)| = q\cdot |Y_0(\mathbb{F}_q)|\), whence the divisibility.
Cohomological translation
The higher direct image sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) are
\[ \mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathbb{Q}_\ell = \begin{cases} \mathbb{Q}_\ell(-1) & \text{if } i = 2 \\ 0 & \text{for } i\ne 2 \end{cases} \]
The Leray spectral sequence of \(f\) therefore degenerates into an isomorphism
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{i-2}(Y,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)(-1) \text{.} \]

To understand the effect of a Tate twist on the eigenvalues of Frobenius, the most convenient thing is to use the Galois point of view ([II]Rapport 1.8), and to note that the Frobenius substitution \(\varphi\) acts on \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell(1)\) by multiplication by \(q\). The eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\) are therefore the products by \(q\) of the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) acting on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{i-2}(Y,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\). We know that these are algebraic integers [16]; hence

\[ \tag{*} \substack{\displaystyle\text{the eigenvalues of } F^\ast \text{ acting on } \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \text{ are} \\ \displaystyle\text{algebraic integers divisible by } q \text{.}} \]
Descent

Let us return to the hypotheses of the theorem. For suitable \(n\), we may suppose that \(\rho\), \(Y\) and \(f\) are defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\). Since the Frobenius morphism relative to \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\) is the \(n\)-th power of the one relative to \(\mathbb{F}_q\), the statement (*) for the scheme over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\) deduced from \(X_0\) by extension of scalars provides us with:

\[ \tag{**} \substack{\displaystyle\text{the } n \text{-th powers of the eigenvalues of } F^\ast \text{ acting on} \\ \displaystyle\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \text{ are algebraic integers divisible by } q^n \text{.}} \]

This assertion implies (*). The number of rational points of \(X_0\), namely \(\sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell))\), is therefore an algebraic integer divisible by \(q\). This implies that it is divisible by \(q\) as a rational integer.

Formula 1.9.3 controls the dependence on \(n\) of the trigonometric sum on the left-hand side. It implies identities between a trigonometric sum and those deduced from it by “extension of the scalars.” The most famous of these identities is that of Hasse-Davenport: let \(\chi:\mathbb{F}_q^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{C}^\times\) and \(\psi:\mathbb{F}_q\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{C}^\times\) be characters, \(\psi\) non-trivial, and let us define the Gauss sum \(\tau(\chi,\psi)\) by
\[ \tag{1.14.1} \tau(\chi,\psi) = - \sum_{x\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times} \psi(x) \chi^{-1}(x) \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.15 (Hasse-Davenport)

We have

\[ \tag{1.15.1} \tau\left(\chi\circ N_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q}\right) = \tau(\chi,\psi)^n \text{.} \]

Let \(E\subset \mathbb{C}\) be a number field containing the values of \(\chi\) and \(\psi\), and \(E_\lambda\) the completion of \(E\) at a place of characteristic \(\ell\ne p\). The identity (1.15.1) is an identity in \(E\). It amounts to the same thing to prove it in \(\mathbb{C}\), or in \(E_\lambda\). We shall prove it in \(E_\lambda\), regarding \(\chi\) and \(\psi\) as taking values in \(E_\lambda^\times\).

We apply 1.9.3 for \(X_0=\mathbb{G}_m\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(G_0=\mathbb{G}_m\times \mathbb{G}_a\). The \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\psi))\) are zero for \(i\ne 1\), and the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1\) is of dimension \(1\) (4.2). By 1.9.3, \(\tau(\chi\circ N_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_q})\) is the unique eigenvalue of \((F^\ast)^n\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1\), and (1.15.1) follows.
Analogous examples are given in Weil [43].

An \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}_0\) on \(X-0\) is said to be pointwise of weight \(n\) if for every closed point \(x\in |X_0|\), the eigenvalues of \(F_x^\ast\) ([II]Rapport 1.2) are algebraic numbers all of whose complex conjugates have absolute value \(q_x^{n/2}\), where \(q_x\) is the number of elements of \(k(x)\). The theorem below will be proved in [15].

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.17

If \(\mathscr{F}_0\) is pointwise of weight \(n\), then for every eigenvalue \(\alpha\) of the endomorphism \(F^\ast\) of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\), there exists an integer \(m\leqslant n+i\) such that the complex conjugates of \(\alpha\) all have absolute value \(q^{m/2}\).
The sheaves considered in 1.9 are of weight \(0\). The theorem therefore provides, for the sum 1.9.1 (or rather, for all its complex conjugates), the bound

\[ \tag{1.17.1} \left|\sum_{s\in S_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \prod_i \chi_i(f^i(s)) \right| \leqslant \sum_i \dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i\left(S,\mathscr{F}\left(\prod \chi_i f^i\right)\right)\cdot q^{i/2} \text{.} \]
1.18 Remarks

1. If \(\dim S=n\), then for every \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(S\), we have

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(S,\mathscr{F}) = 0 \qquad \text{for } i\notin [0,2n] \text{.} \]

  2. The group \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^0(X,\mathscr{F})\) is the group of global sections of \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(S\) whose support is proper. If \(S\) is connected, non-complete and \(\mathscr{F}\) smooth, or if \(S\) is connected, \(\mathscr{F}\) smooth of rank one, and non-constant, then this group is zero.

  3. If \(S\) is smooth purely of dimension \(n\), and \(\mathscr{F}\) smooth, then the Poincaré duality says that the vector spaces \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2n-i}(X,\mathscr{F}^\vee)(2n)\) are dual to each other (for the effect of a Tate twist on the eigenvalues of Frobenius, cf. the \(2\)nd part of the proof of 1.13).

  4. If \(\dim S=n\), Poincaré duality makes it possible to compute as follows \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2n}(S,\mathscr{F})\): one takes an open subset \(U\) of \(S_\text{red}\), whose complement is of dimension \(<n\), smooth purely of dimension \(n\), and on which \(\mathscr{F}\) is smooth. One then has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2n}(U,\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2n}(S,\mathscr{F})\), since in the long exact cohomology sequence, \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(S\setminus U,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(i=2n,2n-1\). By Poincaré, one therefore has

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2n}(S,\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \left(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(U,\mathscr{F}^\vee)(2n)\right)^\vee \text{.} \]

    Suppose \(U\) connected, and let \(u\) be a geometric point of \(U\). The “local system” \(\mathscr{F}\) corresponds to a representation of \(\pi_1(U,u)\) on \(\mathscr{F}_u\), and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(U,\mathscr{F}^\vee)\) is \((\mathscr{F}_u^\vee)^{\pi_1(U,u)}=((\mathscr{F}_u)_{\pi_1(U,u)})^\vee\) (dual of the coinvariants). One therefore has

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{2n}(S,\mathscr{F}) \simeq (\mathscr{F}_u)_{\pi_1(U,u)}(-2n) \text{.} \]

  5. These remarks often make it possible to compute \(b_0\) and \(b_{2n}\). Computing the other \(b_i\) can be difficult. If \(b_{2n}=0\) and \(b_{2n-1}=0\), the bound (1.17.1) is a Lang-Weil-type bound, with, for \(q\) large, a gain of \(\sqrt q\) compared with the trivial bound \(O(q^n)\). One should nevertheless take care that the bound (1.17.1) does not formally imply the trivial bound

    \[ \left|\sum_{s\in S_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \prod_i \chi_i(f^i(s))\right| \leqslant \left| S_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\right| \text{,} \]

    so it can be useful to take it into account (cf. the proof of 3.8).

I explain below a method for proving that \(b_i=0\) for \(i\ne n\). When it applies, it provides an estimate \(O(q^{n/2}\). The implicit constant in \(0\) is \(b_n=(-1)^n \chi(S,\mathscr{F}(\prod \chi_i f^i))\) and can be difficult to compute.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.19

Let \(\overline{X}\) be a proper scheme over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(j:X\hookrightarrow bar X\) an open subset of \(X\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X\). Suppose that

  1. \((j_\ast\mathscr{F})_x = 0\) for \(x\in \overline{X}\setminus X\), i.e. \(j_!\mathscr{F}\xrightarrow{\sim} j_\ast\mathscr{F}\);

  2. \(\mathsf{R}^i j_\ast \mathscr{F} = 0\) for \(i>0\).

Then the maps

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \]

are isomorphisms.
Hypotheses a) b) mean that \(j_! \mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathscr{F}\), whence

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_!\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{H}^i(\overline{X},\mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
In other words, the Leray spectral sequence for \(j\)
\[ E_2^{pq} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(\overline{X},\mathsf{R}^q j_\ast \mathscr{F}) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \]
degenerates, by b), into isomorphisms
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_\ast\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \text{,} \]
while, by a)

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_!\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_\ast\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]

If \(X\) is a curve, or if \(\overline{X}\) is smooth, \(X\) the complement of a divisor with normal crossings and \(\mathscr{F}\) tamely ramified, hypothesis a) of 1.19 (no invariants under the local monodromy) implies hypothesis b).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.20

Let \(X_0\) be a smooth affine scheme purely of dimension \(n\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) a smooth \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf pointwise of weight \(m\) on \(X_0\). Suppose that the maps \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) are isomorphisms (cf. 1.17). Then \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = 0\) for \(i\ne n\), and the complex conjugates of the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(X,\mathscr{F})\) have absolute value \(q^{(m+n)/2}\).

Poincaré duality puts \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) (resp. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}^\vee)\)) in duality with \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2n-i}(X,\mathscr{F}^\vee(n))\) (resp. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2n-i}(X,\mathscr{F}(n))\)). By [2], the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\) without support are zero for \(i>n\). By duality, the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i\) are zero for \(i<n\); since \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F})\), these groups are zero for \(i\ne n\). Let us apply 1.15 to \(\mathscr{F}_0\) and to \(\mathscr{F}_0^\vee(n)\) (of weight \(-m-2n\)). We find that the complex conjugates \(\alpha\) of the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(X,\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(X,\mathscr{F}^\vee(n))^\vee\) satisfy
\begin{align*} |\alpha| &\leqslant q^{(m+n)/2} && \text{and} \\ |\alpha^{-1}| &\leqslant q^{((-m-2n)+n)/2} = q^{-(m+n)/2} \text{,} \end{align*}
whence the assertion.

The last argument shows that if \(X_0\) is a smooth separated scheme over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), that \(\mathscr{F}_0\) is a smooth \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf pointwise of weight \(m\) on \(X_0\) and that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \hookrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F})\), then the complex conjugates of the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) have absolute value \(q^{(m+i)/2}\).
Appendix. The Lang isogeny in the non-commutative case

Let \(G-0\) be a connected algebraic group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\mathfrak{L}\) the morphism \(x\mapsto F x\cdot x^{-1}\) from \(G-0\) into itself. It is a morphism of homogeneous \(G_0\)-spaces, if at the source one lets \(G-0\) act by left translation \(x\mapsto (y\mapsto x y)\), at the target by \(x\mapsto (y\mapsto F x\cdot y\cdot x^{-1}\)). We have \(\mathfrak{L}(xy) = \mathfrak{L}(x)\) for \(y\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(\mathfrak{L}\) induces an isomorphism \(G_0/G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\xrightarrow{\sim} G_0\).

As in the commutative case, \(\mathfrak{L}\) thus makes \(G_0\) into a \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\)-torsor over \(G_0\), the Lang torsor \(L\). If \(\rho:G_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{gl}(n,E_\lambda)\) is a linear representation of \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), we denote by \(\mathscr{F}(\rho)\) the \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf \(\rho(L)\) (1.2).

Let \(\gamma\in G^F=G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and let us compute the endomorphism \(F^\ast\) of \(\mathscr{F}(\rho)_\gamma\). Let \(g\in G\) be such that \(\mathfrak{L}(g)=\gamma\), whence a frame \(\rho(g)\in \operatorname{Isom}(E_\lambda^n,\mathscr{F}(\rho)_\gamma)\). For \(e\in E_\lambda^n\), we have
\[ F(\rho(g)(e)) = \rho(F g)(e) = \rho(\gamma g)(e) = \rho(g\cdot g^{-1}\gamma g)(e) \text{.} \]
We shall see that \(g^{-1} \gamma g\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), whence
\[ F(\rho(g)(e)) = \rho(g) \rho(g^{-1}\gamma g)(e) \]
and
\[ \tag{1.23.1} \rho(g)^{-1} (F_\gamma^\ast)^{-1} \rho(g) = \rho(g^{-1} \gamma g) \text{:} \]
\(\rho(g)\) identifies the inverse of \(F^\ast\) at \(\gamma\) with the automorphism \(\rho(g^{-1} \gamma g)\) of \(E_\lambda^n\). It remains to understand what \(g^{-1} \gamma g\) is.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.24

  1. If \(F g\cdot g^{-1} \in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), then \(g^{-1} (F g\cdot g^{-1}) g = g^{-1} F g\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\).

  2. Let \(\gamma\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(g\) such that \(F g\cdot g^{-1} = \gamma\). The conjugacy class of \(\gamma'=g^{-1} Fg\) in \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\) depends only on that of \(\gamma\).

  3. The map induced by \(\gamma\mapsto \gamma'\), from the set \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)^\natural\) of conjugacy classes of \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\) into itself, is bijective. Its inverse is the map for the opposite group.

(i) If \(\gamma= F g\cdot g^{-1}\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), the identities \(F g=\gamma g\) and \(F\gamma=\gamma\) give \(F(g^{-1} F g) = (F g)^{-1} F F g = g^{-1} \gamma^{-1} F(\gamma g) = g^{-1} \gamma^{-1} F \gamma F g = g^{-1} F g\), so that \(g^{-1} F g \in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\).

(ii) For \(\alpha,\gamma\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), the \(g\) such that \(F g\cdot g^{-1} = \gamma\) form a right coset under \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and if \(F g\cdot g^{-1} = \gamma\), we have \(F(\alpha g \alpha^{-1})(\alpha g \alpha^{-1})^{-1} = \alpha \gamma\alpha^{-1}\). As \(\gamma\) runs through a conjugacy class in \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), the \(g\) such that \(F g\cdot g^{-1} = \gamma\) thus run through a double coset under \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(\gamma'= g^{-1} F g\) runs through a conjugacy class.
(iii) Finally, the inverse of \(F g\cdot g^{-1}\mapsto g^{-1} F g\) is \(g^{-1} F g\mapsto F g\cdot g^{-1}\).

Formula (1.23.1) can be read, briefly: \(F^\ast\) at \(\gamma\) is \(\rho(\gamma')^{-1}\). If \(\gamma\) belongs to the identity component of its centralizer, one can take \(g\) in \(Z(\gamma)\). One then has \(\gamma=\gamma'\). If this condition is not fulfilled, \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\) may fail to be conjugate.
1.26 An example

For \(G_0=\operatorname{SL}(2)\), \(q\) odd, \(\alpha\in F_q^\times\setminus {\mathbb{F}_q^\times}^2\) and \(\overline{\gamma}\) the conjugacy class of \(-1(1+N)\), with \(N^2=0\), \(\overline{\gamma}'\) is the conjugacy class of \(-1\cdot (1+\alpha N)\), so that \(\overline{\gamma}'\ne \overline{\gamma}\) if \(N\ne 0\).
2 Dictionary

An elementary manipulation of trigonometric sums can often be viewed as the reflection, via the trace formula, of a cohomological statement. In this section, I list such statements, and their reflection; they carry the same number, augmented by a \(\ast\) for the cohomological statement.
“A sum of algebraic integers is an algebraic integer” admits as cohomological analogue the following theorem, proved in [16] (cf. the use of 2.1\(^\ast\) in 1.13).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.1 (2.1*)

Let \(X_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X_0\). If, for every \(x\in |X_0|\), the eigenvalues of \(F_x^\ast\) on \(\mathscr{F}_0\) are algebraic integers, then the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) are algebraic integers.
Other integrality results are proved in [16]: if \(\dim(x_0)\leqslant n\), and \(\alpha\) is an eigenvalue of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\), we have:

1. under the hypotheses of 2.1\(^\ast\), and if \(i>n\), then \(q^{i-n}\) divides \(\alpha\);

  2. if the inverses of the eigenvalues of \(F_x^\ast\) are algebraic integers, then \(\alpha^{-1}\) is integral, except at \(p\). More precisely, \(q^{\inf(n,i)}\alpha^{-1}\) is an algebraic integer.
For the sheaves considered in 1.9, the eigenvalues of the \(F_x^\ast\) are roots of unity, so that the hypotheses of the theorem and that of b) above are satisfied.
Let \(f:A\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} B\) be a map from one finite set to another, and \(\varepsilon\) a function on \(A\). We have
\[ \tag{2.3.1} \sum_{a\in A} \varepsilon(a) = \sum_{b\in B} \sum_{f(a)=b} \varepsilon(a) \text{.} \]

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a morphism of separated schemes of finite type over \(k\) algebraically closed, and \(\mathscr{F}\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X\). The Leray spectral sequence of \(f\) in cohomology with proper support is written
\begin{align*} \tag{2.3.1*} E_2^{p q} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(Y,\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \(f_0:X_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_0\) be a morphism of separated schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X_0\). Between (2.3.1) and (2.3.1*) we have the following compatibility.

1. The sheaf \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\) is obtained by extension of scalars from \(\mathbb{F}_q\) to \(\mathbb{F}\) from the sheaf \(\mathsf{R}^q f_{0!} \mathscr{F}_0\) on \(Y_0\). As such, it is equipped with a Frobenius correspondence \(F^\ast:F^\ast\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\). It is obtained by functoriality of \(\mathsf{R} f_!\) from the Frobenius correspondence of \(\mathscr{F}\): it is the composite

    \[ \xymatrix{ F^\ast \mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R}^q f_! F^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F} . } \]

  2. The trace formula for \(\mathscr{F}_q\) is written

    \begin{align*} \tag{1} \sum_{x\in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \operatorname{tr}(F_x^\ast,\mathscr{F}_0) = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})) \text{;} \end{align*}

    that for \(\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}\) is written

    \begin{align*} \tag{2$_q$} \sum_{y\in Y_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \operatorname{tr}(F_y^\ast,\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}) = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast, \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y,\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F})) \text{.} \end{align*}
We have, for \(y\in Y(\mathbb{F})\), \((\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F})_y = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(f^{-1}(y),\mathscr{F})\), and if \(y\in Y_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\),
\[ \operatorname{tr}(F_y^\ast,\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}) = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(f^{-1}(y),\mathscr{F})) \text{,} \]
whence, by the trace formula on the fibre,
\[ \sum_{\substack{x\in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \\ f(x) = y}} \operatorname{tr}(F_x^\ast,\mathscr{F}_0) = \sum (-1)^q \operatorname{tr}(F_y^\ast,\mathsf{R}^q f_! \mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
Taking the alternating sum of the identities (\(2_q\)), we thus find

\begin{align*} \tag{2} \sum_{y\in Y_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \sum_{\substack{x \in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \\ f(x) = y}} \operatorname{tr}(F_x^\ast,\mathscr{F}_0) = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(Y,\mathsf{R}^\bullet f_! \mathscr{F})) \text{.} \end{align*}

The equality of the left-hand sides of (1) and (2) follows from (2.3.1), that of the right-hand sides from (2.3.1*) (taking into account that \(F^\ast\) is an endomorphism of the whole spectral sequence).

Let \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of finite sets, \(A=\prod_{i\in I} A_i\), \(\varepsilon_i\) a function on \(A_i\), and \(\varepsilon\) the function \(a\mapsto \prod \varepsilon_i(a_i)\) on \(A\). We have
\begin{align*} \tag{2.4.1} \sum_{a\in A} \varepsilon(a) = \prod_{i\in I} \sum_{a_i\in A_i} \varepsilon_i(a_i) \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of separated schemes of finite type over \(k\) algebraically closed, \(X=\prod_{i\in I} X_i\), \(\mathscr{F}_i\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X_i\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) the external tensor product \(\boxtimes_{i\in I}\mathscr{F}_i = \bigotimes_{i\in I} \mathrm{pr}_i^\ast(\mathscr{F}_i)\) of the \(\mathscr{F}_i\). We have the Künneth formula
\begin{align*} \tag{2.4.1*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F}) = \bigotimes_{i\in I} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X_i,\mathscr{F}_i) \text{.} \end{align*}

If one wants an isomorphism (2.4.1*) that is canonical, and independent of the choice of a total ordering on \(I\), one must take on the right-hand side the graded tensor product in the sense of the Koszul rule ([IV]Cycle, 1.3).
Let \(A\) be a finite set, \(B\) a subset of \(A\) and \(\varepsilon\) a function on \(A\). We have
\begin{align*} \tag{2.5.1} \sum_{a\in A} \varepsilon(a) = \sum_{a\in A\setminus B}\varepsilon(a) + \sum_{a\in B} \varepsilon(a) \text{.} \end{align*}
Let \(x\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(k\) algebraically closed, \(Y\) a closed subscheme and \(\mathscr{F}\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X\). We have a long exact cohomology sequence

\begin{align*} \tag{2.5.1*} \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X\setminus Y,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(Y,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r]^-\partial & \cdots } \end{align*}

More generally, if one starts from a finite filtration of \(X\) by closed subsets \(X_p\) (\(p\in \mathbb{Z}\); one assumes that \(X_p\supset X_{p+1}\), that \(X_p=X\) for \(p\) small enough, and that \(X_p=\varnothing\) for \(p\) large enough), we have a spectral sequence
\begin{align*} \tag{2.5.2*} E_1^{p q} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+1}(X_p\setminus X_{p+1},\mathscr{F}) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \(A\) be a finite set, \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) a finite covering of \(A\) and \(\varepsilon\) a function on \(A\). For \(J\subset I\), let \(A_J\) be the intersection of the \(A_j\) (\(j\in J\)). We have
\begin{align*} \tag{2.6.1} \sum_{J\subset I} (-1)^{|J|} \sum_{a\in A_J} \varepsilon(a) = 0 \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(k\) algebraically closed, \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) a finite closed (resp. open) covering of \(X\) by subschemes, and \(\mathscr{F}\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X\). For \(J\subset I\), let \(X_J\) be the intersection of the \(X_j\) (\(j\in J\)). We have respective (Leray) spectral sequences

\begin{align*} \tag{2.6.1*} E_1^{p q} &= \bigoplus_{|J|=p+1>0} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X_J,\mathscr{F}) \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \textstyle\bigwedge^{|J|} \mathbb{Z}^J \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \\ \tag{2.6.2*} E_1^{p q} &= \bigoplus_{|J|=1-p>0} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X_J,\mathscr{F}) \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \textstyle\bigwedge^{|J|} \mathbb{Z}^J \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \end{align*}

If \(J=\varnothing\) were not excluded, one would similarly have spectral sequences converging to \(0\). The factors \(\bigwedge^{|J|} \mathbb{Z}^J\) are there to spare us from choosing a total ordering on \(I\).
Let \(A\) be a finite commutative group, and \(\chi:A \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\) a non-trivial character. We have
\begin{align*} \tag{2.7.1} \sum_{a\in A} \chi(a) = 0 \text{.} \end{align*}
We shall prove the cohomological analogue of (2.7.1) by transposing the following proof: if \(x\in A\), \(a\mapsto x a\) is a permutation of \(A\), and
\begin{align*} \sum_{a\in A}\chi(a) = \sum_{a\in A} \chi(x a) &= \chi(x) \sum_{a\in A} \chi(a) && \text{, hence} \\ (\chi(x)-1)\sum_{a\in A} &= 0 \text{,} \end{align*}
and by hypothesis there exists \(x\) such that \(\chi(x)-1\ne 0\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.7 (2.7*)

Let \(G_0\) be a connected commutative algebraic group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\chi:G_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\) a non-trivial character. We have

\begin{align*} \tag{2.7.1*} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(G,\mathscr{F}(\chi)) = 0 \text{.} \end{align*}

For \(x\) a rational point of \(G\), let us denote by \(t_x\) the translation \(t_x(g) = x g\) of \(G\). The formula \(\mathfrak{L} t_x = t_{\mathfrak{L}(x)} \mathfrak{L}\) expresses that \((t_x,t_{\mathfrak{L}(x)})\) is an automorphism of the diagram \(G\xrightarrow{\mathfrak{L}} G\) (\(G\) equipped with the Lang torsor). Let \(\rho(g)\) be the automorphism of \((G,\mathscr{F}(\chi))\) deduced from it. For \(g\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), i.e. for \(\mathfrak{L}(g) = e\), it is the identity on \(G\), and multiplication by \(\chi(g)^{-1}\) on \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\).

Let us denote by \(\rho_H(g)\) the automorphism of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(G,\mathscr{F}(\chi))\) deduced from \(\rho(g)\). A homotopy argument (Lemma 2.8 below) shows that \(\rho_H(g) = \rho_H(e)\), hence is the identity. On the other hand, for \(g\in G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), \(\rho_H(g)\) is multiplication by \((\chi^{-1}(g):\text{ on }\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(G,\mathscr{F}(\chi))\), multiplication by \((\chi^{-1}(g)-1)\) is zero. Taking \(g\) such that \(\chi(g)\ne 1\), we obtain 2.7.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.8

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two schemes over \(k\) algebraically closed, with \(X\) separated of finite type and \(Y\) connected. Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be a sheaf on \(X\) and \((\rho,\varepsilon)\) a family of endomorphisms of \((X,\mathscr{F})\) parametrized by \(Y\):

\begin{align*} \rho:Y\times_k X &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\times_k X && \text{is a } Y \text{-morphism, and} \\ \varepsilon:\rho^\ast \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast \mathscr{F} &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast\mathscr{F} && \text{a morphism of sheaves.} \end{align*}

Suppose that \(\rho\) is proper. For \(y\in Y(k)\), let \(\rho_H(y)^\ast\) be the endomorphism of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})\) induced by \(\rho_y:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) and \(\varepsilon_y:\rho_y^\ast\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}\). Then \(\rho_H(y)^\ast\) is independent of \(y\).

Indeed, \(\mathsf{R}^p \mathrm{pr}_{1!} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast\mathscr{F}\) is the constant sheaf on \(Y\) with value \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(X,\mathscr{F})\), and \(\rho_H(y)^\ast\) is the fibre at \(y\) of the endomorphism

\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}^p \mathrm{pr}_{1!} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r]^-{\rho^\ast} & \mathsf{R}^p \mathrm{pr}_{1!} \rho^\ast \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r]^-\varepsilon & \mathsf{R}^p \mathrm{pr}_{1!} \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast \mathscr{F} } \]
of this sheaf.
2.9 Remark

Let \(G_0\) be a connected algebraic group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and \(\rho:G_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{GL}(V)\) a linear representation such that \(V^{G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)}=0\). We again have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(G,\rho(L))=0\).
3 Sums in one variable

Weil was the first to apply “cohomological” methods to the study of trigonometric sums in one variable; since he had proved the analogue of the Riemann hypothesis for Artin \(L\)-functions over function fields, these methods provided him with excellent estimates (in \(O(\text{square root of the number of terms})\)), and the behaviour of these sums under “extension of the base field.”
The bulk of this section is an account, in cohomological language, of his results.

The cohomological methods here lead to computing groups \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\), for \(\mathscr{F}_0\) an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on a curve \(X-0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). These groups are zero for \(i\ne 0,1,2\) and for \(i=0,2\), they have a simple interpretation (1.8 a,b,c). Moreover, the Euler-Poincaré characteristic \(\chi_c(\mathscr{F}) = \sum (-1)^i \dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) (equal moreover to \(\chi(\mathscr{F}) = \sum (-1)^i \dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) can be computed in terms of \(x\), of the rank of \(\mathscr{F}\) at the generic points of \(X\), and of the ramification properties of \(\mathscr{F}\). The essential result is the following.

Let \(\overline{X}\) be a smooth connected projective curve, of genus \(g\), over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(X\) a dense open subset of \(\overline{X}\), the complement of a finite set \(S\) of points and \(\mathscr{F}\) a smooth \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf on \(X\). Let \(\chi(X)=2-2 g-\# S\) be the Euler-Poincaré characteristic of \(X\), and \(\operatorname{rg}(\mathscr{F})\) the rank of \(\mathscr{F}\). For each point \(s\in S\), one defines an integer \(\operatorname{Sw}_s(\mathscr{F})\), the Swan conductor, measuring the wild ramification of \(\mathscr{F}\), and
\begin{align*} \tag{3.2.1} \chi_c(\mathscr{F}) = \operatorname{rg}(\mathscr{F}) \cdot \chi(X) - \sum_{s\in S} \operatorname{Sw}_s(\mathscr{F}) \end{align*}
[29].

Let \(\overline{X}\), \(j:X\hookrightarrow\overline{X}\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) be as in 3.2. The Poincaré duality theorem admits the very convenient form: \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_\ast \mathscr{F})\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2-i}(\overline{X},j_\ast(\mathscr{F}^\vee(1)))\) are dual to each other ([V]Dualité, 1.3).

Let \(k=\mathbb{F}\), and suppose that \(X\), \(\overline{X}\), and \(\mathscr{F}\) come from \(X_0\), \(\overline{X}_0\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). If \(\mathscr{F}_0\) becomes trivial on a finite covering of \(X_0\), Weil proved that the complex conjugates of the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_\ast\mathscr{F})\) have absolute value \(q^{i/2}\). Such sheaves \(\mathscr{F}_0\) correspond to Artin \(L\)-functions over the function field of \(\overline{X}_0\).

Under the same hypotheses, or more generally if \(E_\lambda\) is the completion at a place \(\lambda\) of a number field \(E\) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) belongs to an infinite compatible system of \(v\)-adic representations (\(v\) a place of \(E\)), one can compute
\[ \prod_i \det(-F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}))^{(-1)^i} \]

from local information about \(\mathscr{F}_0\). This is explained in [13]. For \(\mathscr{F}_0\) trivial on a finite covering of \(X_0\), it is the expression of the constant of the functional equation of an Artin \(L\)-function as a product of local constants.
3.5 Example

Let \(\psi\) be the character \(\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{p} \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p}\right)\) of \(\mathbb{F}_q\); we have \(\psi(a^p-a)=0\). Let \(X_0\) be a smooth absolutely irreducible projective curve of genus \(g\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(f\) a rational function on \(X_0\), i.e. a morphism \(f:X_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{P}^1\), not identically equal to \(\infty\). We are interested in the sum
\[ S_f' = \sum_{\substack{x\in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q) \\ f(x)\ne \infty}} \psi(f(x)) \text{.} \]
This sum is zero for \(f\) of the form \(g^p-g\). This suggests modifying the sum \(S_f'\) as follows:

1. for every closed point \(x\) of \(X_0\), we set \(v_x(f) = \) order of the pole of \(f\) at \(x\) if \(f(x)=\infty\), \(v_x(f)=0\) otherwise, and \(v_x^\ast(f) = \inf v_x(f+g^p-g)\) (infimum over \(g\)).

  2. If \(v_x^\ast(f)=0\), \(x\in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(f+g^p-g\) is regular at \(x\), we set \(\psi(f(x)) = \psi((f+g^p-g)(x))\). We finally set

    \[ \tag{3.5.1} S_f = \sum'_{x\in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)} \psi(f(x)) \text{,} \]

    where \((-)'\) indicates that the sum is extended to the \(x\) such that \(v_x^\ast(f)=0\).
We have \(S_f=S_{f+g^p-g}\). We propose to verify that if \(f\) is not of the form \(g^p-g+c^{t e}\), then
\[ \tag{3.5.2} |S_f|\leqslant \left(2 g-2+\sum_{v_x^\ast(f)\ne 0} [k(x):\mathbb{F}_q] (1+v_x^\ast(f))\right) q^{1/2} \text{.} \]

We begin by passing from the complex to the \(\ell\)-adic, replacing \(\psi\) by a character of the form \(\psi_0\circ \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p}\), with \(\psi_0:\mathbb{F}_p\hookrightarrow E_\lambda^\times\). For \(j:U_0\hookrightarrow X_0\) the inclusion of the open set where \(f\ne\infty\), one then proves that
\[ \tag{3.5.3} S_f = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f))) \text{.} \]
The trace formula reduces this statement to the following (for \(x\in X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\)):

1. If \(v_x^\ast(f)=0\), then \(F_x^\ast\) on \(j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f)\) is \(\psi(f(x))\);

  2. If \(v_x^\ast(f)\ne 0\), then \(j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f)\) ramifies at \(x\): \((j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f))_{\overline{x}}=0\).

Formula a) follows from (1.7.6) if \(v_x(f)=0\), and one reduces to this case by replacing \(f\) by \(f+g^p-g\): up to isomorphism, this does not change \(\mathscr{F}(\psi f)_0\) on the open set where \(f\) and \(g\) are regular (1.3).
Formula b) follows from
\[ \tag{3.5.4} \operatorname{Sw}_x \mathscr{F}(f,\psi) = v_x^\ast(f) \text{.} \]
After reduction to the case where \(v_x(f)=v_x^\ast(f)\) (whence \(p\nmid v_x(f)\)) and extension of scalars to \(\mathbb{F}\), this formula is in [34].

Finally, one verifies that the sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi f)\) on \(U\) is non-constant if \(f\) is not of the form \(g^p-g+c^{t e}\): since \(\psi_0\) is injective, the triviality of \(\mathscr{F}(\psi f)=\mathscr{F}(\psi_0 f)\) (1.8.ii) is equivalent to that of the \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-torsor whose equation would be the inverse image of a \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-torsor on \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_q)\), of equation \(T^p-T-\lambda=0\), the \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-torsor of equation \(T^p-T-(f-\lambda)=0\) on \(U_0\) would be trivial and \(f\) would thus be of the form \(g^p-g+\lambda\). The \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f))\) are thus zero for \(i\ne 1\), formula (3.5.3) reduces to
\[ \tag{3.5.5} S_f = -\operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\overline{X},j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f))) \]

and, by (3.2.1) and (3.5.4), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\) has dimension \(2 g-2+\sum_{v_x^\ast(f)>0} [k(x):\mathbb{F}_q](1+v_x^\ast(f))\) and \(-S_f\) is the sum of this number of eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\), each of complex absolute value \(q^{1/2}\).
Suppose that, for an automorphism \(\sigma\) of \(X_0\), one has
\[ f(\sigma x) = - f(x) \text{.} \]

The sum \(S_f\) is then real. If \(\sigma\) is involutive, Poincaré duality allows us to say a little more: if we set \(\mathscr{F}_0=j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi f)\), \(\mathscr{G}_0 = j_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi(-f))\), we have

1. \(\mathscr{F}_0\) and \(\mathscr{G}_0\) are in duality,

  2. \(\sigma^\ast \mathscr{F}_0 \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{G}_0\) and \(\sigma^\ast \mathscr{G}_0 \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{F}_0\), for natural isomorphisms such that the composite \(\mathscr{F}_0=(\sigma^2)^\ast \mathscr{F}_0 \xrightarrow{\sim} \sigma^\ast \mathscr{G}_0 \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{F}_0\) is the identity.

  3. The pairing \(\mathscr{F}_0\otimes \mathscr{G}_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda\) satisfies \(\sigma^\ast(f\cdot g) = \sigma^\ast(f) \cdot \sigma^\ast (g)\).

Passing to cohomology, we find that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) are in perfect duality with values in \(E_\lambda(1)\), and that the bilinear form \(\alpha\cdot \sigma^\ast\beta\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) is alternating: \(\sigma^\ast\) acts trivially on \(E_\lambda(1)\), and
\[ \alpha\cdot \sigma^\ast \beta = \sigma^\ast(\alpha\cdot \sigma^\ast \beta) = \sigma^\ast \alpha\cdot \beta = -\beta\cdot \sigma^\ast \alpha \text{.} \]

We conclude from this that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) is of even dimension (one moreover verifies easily that each non-zero \(v_x^\ast(f)\) is odd) and that the eigenvalues of \(F^\ast\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\) are grouped in pairs \(\alpha\) and \(q/\alpha\).
3.7 Example

This applies to the Kloosterman sums \(\sum_{x\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times} \psi\left(x+\frac a x\right)\) (take \(X_0=\mathbb{P}^1\), \(f=x+\frac a x\), \(\sigma x=-x\); the poles of \(f\) are \(0\) and \(\infty\), and at each of them \(v_x^\ast(f)=1\); the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\) has dimension \(-2+2+2=2\)). We thus have (for \(a\ne 0\))

\[ \sum_{\substack{x y=a \\ x,y\in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}}} \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{p} \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n}/\mathbb{F}_p}(x+y)\right) = (-\alpha^n+\alpha^{-n}) \qquad \text{, }\alpha\overline{\alpha} = q \text{.} \]
This result is due to L. Carlitz [9].
Here now is an application of a method of Lang-Weil.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.8

Let \(P\in \mathbb{F}_q[X_1,\dots,X_n]\) be a polynomial in \(n\) variables, of degree \(d\), which is assumed not to be of the form \(Q^p-Q+C^{te}\). Setting again \(\psi(x) = \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{p} \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)\right)\) we have

\[ \left|\sum_{x_i\in \mathbb{F}_q} \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| \leqslant (d+1) q^{n-\frac 1 2} \text{.} \]

For the left-hand side we have the trivial estimate \(q^n\). It thus suffices to prove 3.8 when \(d-1<q^{1/2}\); suppose only that \(d<q+1\), and let \(P_d\) be the homogeneous part of degree \(d\) of \(P\). Let us recall the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.9

A hypersurface of degree \(d\) in \(\mathbb{P}^r\) (\(r\geqslant i\)) cannot pass through all the rational points over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) unless \(d\geqslant q+1\).

One proceeds by induction: if there exists a rational hyperplane not entirely contained in the hypersurface (which is not the case for \(r=1\)), one applies the induction hypothesis to the trace of the hypersurface on this hyperplane. Otherwise, the degree \(d\) is \(\geqslant\) the number of rational hyperplanes, \(\geqslant q+1\).
Let us now distinguish two cases.
Case 1: \(p\nmid d\).

Applying the lemma to \(P_d\), we see that, after a linear change of variables, we may assume that \(P_d(1,0,\ldots,0)\ne 0\), i.e. that the coefficient of \(X_1^d\) in \(P\) is non-zero. A polynomial in \(1\) variable
\[ S(X) = \sum_{i=0}^d a_i x^i \text{,} \]
with \(a_d\ne 0\) (\(p\nmid d\)) is never of the form \(Q^p-Q+C^{t e}\), and the estimate (3.5.2) reduces to
\[ \left| \sum \psi(S(x)) \right| \leqslant (d-1) q^{1/2} \text{.} \]
Applying this estimate to the partial sums obtained by letting only \(x_1\) vary, we find
\[ \left| \sum \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n) \right| = \left| \sum_{x_2,\dots,x_n} \sum_{x_1} \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| \leqslant q^{n-1} (d-1) q^{1/2} \]
as promised.

If \(P_d\) is a \(p\)-th power, replacing \(P\) by \(P-(P_d-P_d^{1/p})\) does not change the sum under consideration, and lowers the degree: we dispose of this case by proceeding by induction on \(d\). Otherwise, the differential of \(P_d\) is not identically zero; applying 3.9, we may assume, after a linear change of variables, that it is non-zero at the point \((1,0,\dots,0)\). If we write
\[ P_d = \sum_{i=0}^d X_1^{d-i} S_i(X_2,\dots,X_n) \text{,} \]
this means that the linear form \(S_1\) is not identically zero.

The form \(S_0\) is a constant, and replacing \(P\) by \(P-(S_0 X_1^d -S_0^{1/p} X_1^{d/p})\), we may assume that it is zero. Finally, let \(-\lambda\) be the coefficient of \(X_1^{d-1}\) in \(P\). For \(x_2,\dots,x_n\) fixed, we have
\[ P(X_1,x_2,\dots,x_n) = (S_1(x_2,\dots,x_n)-\lambda) X_1^{d-1} + \text{lower-degree terms in } X_1 \]
and if \(S_1(x_2,\dots,x_n)\ne \lambda\), we therefore have
\[ \left| \sum_{x_1} \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| \leqslant (d-2) q^{1/2} \text{.} \]
In total,

\begin{align*} \left|\sum \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| &\leqslant \left|\sum_{S=\lambda} \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| + \sum_{S(X_2,\dots,X_n)\ne\lambda} \left| \sum_{x_1} \psi P(x_1,\dots,x_n)\right| \\ &\leqslant q^{n-1} + (q^{n-1}-q^{n-2})(d-2) q^{1/2} \\ &< (d-2) q^{n-1/2} + q^{n-1} \\ &< (d-1) q^{n-1/2} \text{.} \end{align*}
Another result of this nature is given by R.A. Smith [37].
4 Gauss sums and Jacobi sums

Let \(k\) be a finite field of characteristic \(p\), let \(\chi\) be a character of \(k^\times\), and let \(\psi\) be a non-trivial character of the additive group of \(k\). We shall take as the definition of the Gauss sums:
\[ \tag{4.1.1} \tau(\chi,\psi) = -\sum_{x\in k^\times} \psi(x) \chi^{-1}(x) \]

(note the sign). Classically, \(\chi\) and \(\psi\) are complex-valued. We shall take them with values in \(E_\lambda^\times\) (cf. the proof of 1.15). Let us regard \(-\tau(\chi,\psi)\) as a sum over the rational points of the scheme \(\mathbb{G}_m\) over \(k\). By section 1, we have \(-\tau(\chi,\psi) = \operatorname{tr}(F^\ast,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\ast(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi \chi^{-1}))\). Moreover

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2

The cohomology of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) with coefficients in \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\chi^{-1})\) satisfies

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i=0\) for \(i\ne 1\), and \(\dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1=1\).

  2. \(F^\ast\), acting on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1\), is multiplication by \(\tau(\chi,\psi)\).

  3. If \(\chi\) is non-trivial, we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\).

blocks.title: Preuve
blocks.html:
Proof▾

For every \(n\) prime to \(p\), let \(K_n\) denote the \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\)-torsor on \(\mathbb{G}_m\) defined by the Kummer exact sequence \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{x^n} \mathbb{G}_m \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\). If \(k\) has \(q\) elements, we have over \(k\): \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{q-1}=k^\times\), and the Lang torsor on \(\mathbb{G}_m/k\) is \(K_{q-1}\). Hence \(\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1})=\chi(K_{q-1})\). Assertion 4.2(ii) follows from (i,iii), which are themselves contained in the following geometric statement, where \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) denotes the sheaf on \(\mathbb{G}_m/\mathbb{F}\) deduced by extension of scalars from \(k\) to \(\mathbb{F}\) of \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(\mathbb{G}_m/k\) (1.8.b).

C.Q.F.D.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3

Let \(\chi:\boldsymbol{\mu}_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\). The cohomology of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) with coefficients in \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\otimes \chi(K_n)\) satisfies

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i=0\) for \(i\ne 1\), and \(\dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1{} = 1\).

  2. If \(\chi\) is non-trivial, we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet{}\xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet{}\).

blocks.title: Preuve
blocks.html:
Proof▾

The sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) is the restriction to \(\mathbb{G}_m\) of a locally constant sheaf on \(\mathbb{G}_a\), wildly ramified at infinity, with Swan conductor \(1\). The sheaf \(\chi(K_n)\) is constant if \(\chi=1\); if \(\chi\ne 1\), it is ramified at \(0\) and \(\infty\), tamely.

The sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\otimes\chi(K_n)\) is therefore ramified at \(\infty\); applying 1.18(b,c), we find that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi)\otimes \chi(K_n))=0\) for \(i\ne 1\). If \(\chi\ne 1\), it is ramified at \(0\) and \(\infty\) and (ii) follows from 1.19.a.

The Swan conductors are \(0\) at \(0\) and \(1\) at \(\infty\). By (3.2.1), the Euler-Poincaré characteristic is therefore \(-1\) and this completes the proof.

C.Q.F.D.
4.4 Remark

If \(\chi\) is non-trivial, 4.2(iii) and Poincaré duality show that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi\chi^{-1}))\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi^{-1}\chi))\) are in duality (a duality with values in \(E_\lambda(-1)\)). We therefore have \(\tau(\chi,\psi)\cdot \tau(\chi^{-1},\psi^{-1}) = q\), i.e. \(|\tau(\chi,\psi)|=1\).

If \(k\) is an extension of degree \(N\) of \(\mathbb{F}_q\), we can also regard (4.1.1) as a sum in \(N\) variables over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). More generally, let \(k\) be an étale algebra over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), of degree \(N\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). It is a product of fields \(k_i\), of degree \(N_i\), and we set
\[ \tag{4.5.1} \varepsilon(k) = (-1)^{\sum (N_i+1)} \text{.} \]
This is the signature of the permutation of \(S=\hom_{\mathbb{F}_q}(k,\mathbb{F})\) induced by the Frobenius substitution \(\varphi\in \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{F}_q)\).

Let \(\psi:\mathbb{F}_q\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\) be a non-trivial character, and \(\chi:k^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\). We set
\[ \tag{4.5.2} \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi) = (-1)^N \sum_{x\in k^\times} \psi \operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q}(x) \cdot \chi^{-1}(x) \text{.} \]
If \(\chi\) has coordinates \(\chi_i:k_i^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\), we have the trivial identity
\[ \tag{4.5.3} \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi) = \varepsilon(k) \prod \tau(\chi_i,\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{k_i/\mathbb{F}_q}) \text{.} \]

After a few preliminaries, we shall give in 4.10 a cohomological interpretation of the sums (4.5.2). In 4.12, we shall interpret the Hasse-Davenport identity as a twisted form (cf. 1.12) of the following special case of (4.5.3): for \(k=\mathbb{F}_q^N\), and \(\chi\) a character of \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\), we have \(\tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi)=\tau(\chi,\psi)^N\).

Recall that for \(M\) a projective module of finite type over a ring \(A\), the functor \(\operatorname{Spec}(B)\mapsto M\otimes_A B\), from affine schemes over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) to \(\mathsf{Ens}\), is represented by the affine scheme \(\mathbb{V}(M^\vee)\) (notation of EGA), the spectrum of \(\operatorname{Sym}_A^\bullet(M^\vee)\). If \(M=A^n\), it is the standard affine space of dimension \(n\).

Suppose that \(M\) is an \(A\)-algebra with unit, and set \(V=\mathbb{V}(M^\vee)\). By definition, for every extension \(B\) of \(A\), the set \(V(B)\) of points of \(V\) with coordinates in \(B\) is \(M\otimes_A B\). Since the functor \(B\mapsto M\otimes_A B\) takes values in rings with unit, \(V\) is a scheme of rings with unit over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). The norm and trace morphisms: \(M\otimes_A B\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} B\) are functorial in \(B\); they therefore correspond to scheme morphisms \(N\) and \(T\) from \(V\) into \(\mathbb{G}_a\). We shall have to consider the following schemes deduced from \(V\):

1. \(V^\ast\) is the open set of invertible elements of \(V\) (a group scheme for \(\cdot\));

  2. \(W\) is the hyperplane with equation \(T=0\) and \(W^\ast=W\cap V^\ast\);

  3. \(P\) is the hyperplane at infinity \(V\setminus \{0\}/\mathbb{G}_m\) of the affine space \(V\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). If \(Q\) is the hyperplane at infinity of \(W\), \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) and \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) are open subsets of the projective spaces \(Q\) and \(P\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\).

    \[ \tag{4.6.1} \xymatrix{ W^\ast \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[d]^-\pi & V^\ast \ar[d]^-\pi \\ W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m \ar@{^{(}->}[r] & V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m }\qquad\subset\qquad \xymatrix{ W\setminus \{0\} \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[d]^-\pi & V\setminus \{0\} \ar[d]^-\pi \\ Q \ar@{^{(}->}[r] & P . } \]

If \(M=A^I\), \(I\) a finite set, then \(V\simeq \mathbb{G}_a^I\), \(V^\ast=\mathbb{G}_m^I\), \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) is the torus \(\mathbb{G}_m^I/(\mathbb{G}_m\text{ diagonal})\), \(N\) and \(T\) are written \(\prod x_i\) and \(\sum x_i\), and \(Q\) is therefore the projective hyperplane with equation \(\sum x_i=0\) in \(P\).

The case of interest to us is that in which \(M\) is finite étale over \(A\). The foregoing description then holds locally on \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) (for the étale topology) and we may write \(V^\ast=\mathbb{G}_m^I\), for \(I\) a locally constant sheaf of finite sets on \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). If for example \(A\) is a field, with algebraic closure \(\overline{A}\), and \(M\) is a separable \(A\)-algebra, we set \(I=\hom_A(M,\overline{A})\), and, over \(\overline{A}\), we have \(V\sim \mathbb{G}_a^I\). Via this isomorphism, \(N\) and \(T\) are written \(\prod x_i\) and \(\sum x_i\).
4.7 Kummer torsor
Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(n\) an integer invertible on \(S\) and \(G\) a commutative group scheme with connected fibres (written multiplicatively) over \(S\). The sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & G_n \ar[r] & G \ar[r]^-{x^n} & G \ar[r] & 0 } \]

is exact. It defines a \(G_n\)-torsor \(K_n(G)\) (or simply \(K_n\)) on \(G\). For \(\chi:G_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\) a homomorphism of the étale \(S\)-sheaf \(G_n\) into the constant sheaf \(E_\lambda^\times\), we denote by \(\mathscr{K}_n(\chi)\) the \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf \(\chi^{-1}(K_n)\).

The torsors \(K_n\) form a projective system of torsors under the projective system of groups \(G_n\) (transition morphisms \(x\mapsto x^d:G_{n d}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G_n\)). This expresses the commutativity of the diagrams
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & G_{n d} \ar[r] \ar[d]^-{x^d} & G \ar[r]^-{x^{n d}} \ar[d]^-{x^d} & G \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & G_n \ar[r] & G \ar[r]^-{x^n} & G \ar[r] & 0 . } \]
We therefore have \(\mathscr{K}_n(\chi) = \mathscr{K}_{n d}(\chi\circ x^d)\).

Let us apply the construction 4.6 for \(A=\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(M=k\) an étale algebra over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). In accordance with the general conventions, we shall denote with a subscript \(0\) the \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-schemes denoted \(V,V^\ast,\ldots\) in 4.6. The same letters without subscript denote the schemes over \(\mathbb{F}\) deduced from them by extension of scalars.
We set \(I=\hom(k,\mathbb{F})\), whence \(V\sim \mathbb{G}_a^I\) and \(T\) is written \((x_i)\mapsto \sum x_i\).
\[ \tag{4.8.1} \mathscr{F}(\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q}) = T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi) = \bigotimes_i \mathrm{pr}_i^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi) \text{.} \]

Since \(V^\ast\sim \mathbb{G}+m^I\), a character \(\chi\) of \(V_n^\ast\sim \boldsymbol{\mu}_n^I\), with values in \(E_\lambda^\times\), is written as a family \((\chi_i)_{i\in I}\) of characters of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\) indexed by \(I\). It is defined over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) if, for every \(\sigma\in \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{F}_q)\), we have \(\chi_{\sigma_i} = \chi_i\circ \sigma^{-1}\). It then defines an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\) on \(V_0^\ast\). If the product of the \(\chi_i\) is trivial, \(\chi\) factors through a character of \((V_0^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m)_n\) and \(\mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\) is the inverse image of a sheaf, denoted likewise, on \(V-0^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\). This construction compares as follows with the Lang torsor.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.9

  1. For \(n\) sufficiently divisible, we have a commutative diagram

    \[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & (V_0^\ast)_n \ar[r] \ar[d]^-\tau & V_0^\ast \ar[r]^-{x^n} \ar[d]^-\tau & V_0^\ast \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & k^\times \ar[r] & V_0^\ast \ar[r]^-{\mathfrak{L}} & V_0^\ast \ar[r] & 0 ; } \]

    if \(\chi\) is a character \(\chi:k^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\), we have \(\mathscr{F}(\chi) = \mathscr{K}_n(\chi\circ\tau)\).

  2. For \(n\) sufficiently divisible, \(\tau\) identifies \(k^\times\) with the coinvariants of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}/F)\) acting on \(V_n^\ast\sim \boldsymbol{\mu}_n^I\).

  3. For \(k\) a field, \(N=[k:\mathbb{F}_q]\), \(\omega\in I\) an embedding of \(k\) into \(\mathbb{F}\), and \(n=q^N-1\), the component of index \(\omega\) of \(\chi\circ\tau\) is \(\chi\circ \omega^{-1}\).

  4. If \(\chi\) is non-trivial on each factor of \(k\), the \((\chi\circ \tau)_i\) are all non-trivial.

It suffices to prove the lemma when \(k\) is a field, of degree \(N\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). In this case, \(n\) is "sufficiently divisible" if \(q^N-1\mid n\). Let us choose an embedding \(\omega\) of \(k\) into \(\mathbb{F}_q\); \(I\) then identifies with \(\mathbb{Z}/N\): to \(i\in \mathbb{Z}/N\) corresponds \(\omega_i=\omega^{q^i}\). Via the isomorphism \(V_0^\ast(\mathbb{F}) = {F^\times}^I\), we have

1. \(x\in k^\times\) corresponds to \((\omega_i(x))\in {\mathbb{F}^\times}^I\);

  2. \(F((x_i)_{i\in \mathbb{Z}/N})=(x_{i-1}^q)_{i\in \mathbb{Z}/N}\).

A character \(\chi=(\chi_i)\) of \(V_n^\ast\sim \boldsymbol{\mu}_n^I\) will be defined over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) if \(\chi_{-i} =\chi_0(x^{q^i})\) (\(i\in \mathbb{Z}\)). If \(q^N-1\mid n\), there are \(q^N-1\) such characters: \(\chi_0\) factors through \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{q^N-1}\), and determines the \(\chi_i\). To prove (ii), it therefore suffices to verify (i) and (iii) (or its corollary (iv)) which ensures that \(\chi\mapsto \chi\circ \tau\) is injective.

Let us prove (i) and (iii), for \(n=q^N-1\). Let us write additively the group of endomorphisms of \(V^\ast\sim \mathbb{G}_m^I\); in particular, let us denote by \(n\) the operator \(x\mapsto x^n\). If \(\alpha\) is the circular permutation operator \((x_i)\mapsto (x_{i-1})\), we have \(q^N-1=(q\alpha)^N-1 = (q\alpha-1)((q\alpha)^{N-1}+\cdots + 1)\). This determines \(\tau\): we have \(\tau((x_i)) = \prod_{0\leqslant j<N} x_{i-j}^{q^j}\), and the induced map from \((V_0^\ast)_n\) into \(k^\times\) is written [a) above] \((x_i)\mapsto \prod x_{-i}^{q^i}\); (iii) results from this.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.10

The cohomology of \(V^\ast\) with coefficients in \(\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\cdot \psi\operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q})\) satisfies

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i = 0\) for \(i\ne N\), and \(\dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^N=1\).

  2. On \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^N\), \(F^\ast\) is multiplication by \(\tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi)\).

  3. If \(\chi\) is non-trivial on each factor of \(k\), we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\).

Let us apply 4.9(i): over \(\mathbb{F}\), if \(\chi\circ \tau=(\chi_i)_{i\in I}\), we have \(\mathscr{F}(\chi) = \mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\). Points (i) and (iii) therefore follow from the following more geometric statement (for (iii), apply 4.9(iv)) and (ii) follows from it by the trace formula:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.11

Let \((\chi_i)_{i\in I}\) be a family of characters of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n(\mathbb{F})\). The cohomology of \(V^\ast\simeq \mathbb{G}_m^I\) with coefficients in \(\mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\otimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q})\) satisfies

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i{}=0\) for \(i\ne N\), and \(\dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^N{} = 1\).

  2. If the \(\chi_i\) are all non-trivial, we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet{}\xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet\).

We have \(V^\ast\sim \mathbb{G}_m^I\), \(\mathscr{K}((\chi_i)) = \bigotimes_i \mathrm{pr}_i^\ast \chi_i(K_n(\mathbb{G}_m))\) and \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/k})=T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi) = \bigotimes_i \mathrm{pr}_i^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\). This allows us to apply the Künneth formula, and 4.11 follows from 4.3.

From 2.4* and ([VI]Cycle, 1.3 example 2), we also deduce that the group of permutations \(\sigma\) of \(I\) such that \(\chi_i = \chi_{\sigma i}\) (\(i\in I\)) acts on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^N\) by multiplication by the signature \(\varepsilon(\sigma)\). We shall deduce from it a second proof of the Hasse-Davenport identity.

If \(\chi\) is a character of \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\), the fact that, over \(\mathbb{F}\), \(N\) is written \((x_i)\mapsto \prod x_i\) yields: \(\mathscr{F}(\chi\circ N)=N^\ast\mathscr{F}(\chi) = \bigotimes_i \mathrm{pr}_i^\ast\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) and the Künneth formula yields:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(V^\ast,\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\circ N,\psi\circ \operatorname{tr})) \sim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\psi))^{\otimes I} \text{,} \]

where, on the right-hand side, the tensor product is taken in the sense of 2.4*. Since \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi\chi^{-1}))\) is of dimension \(1\), its \(\otimes I\) tensor power, in the ordinary sense, depends only on the cardinality \(n\) of \(I\). Applying ([IV]Cycle, 1.3 example 2), we obtain a canonical isomorphism

\[ \tag{4.12.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^N\left(V,\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\circ N)\otimes T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\right) \sim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi\chi^{-1})) \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \textstyle \bigwedge^N \mathbb{Z}^I \text{.} \]

To compute the action of \(F^\ast\), the most convenient thing is to adopt the Galois point of view and to say that the isomorphism (4.12.1), being canonical, is compatible with the action by transport of structure of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{F}_q)\). If \(\varepsilon(k)\) is the signature of the permutation \(\varphi\) of \(I\), we find that

\begin{align*} \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi) &= \operatorname{tr}\left(\varphi^{-1},\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^N\left(V^\ast,N^\ast\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1})\otimes T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\right)\right) \\ &= \varepsilon(k) \operatorname{tr}\left(\varphi^{-1},\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\psi))\right)^N \\ &= \varepsilon(k) \tau(\chi,\psi)^N \text{,} \end{align*}
that is
\[ \tag{4.12.2} \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}\left(\chi\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\right) = \varepsilon(k) \tau(\chi,\psi)^N \text{.} \]
If \(k\) is a field, \(\varphi\) is a circular permutation of \(I\), \(\varepsilon(k) = (-1)^{N+1}\), and we recover the Hasse-Davenport identity:

\[ \tau\left(\chi\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q}\right) = (-1)^{N+1} \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}\left(\chi\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\right) = \tau(\chi,\psi)^N \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.13

For \(\chi\circ \tau=(\chi_i)_{i\in I}\) as in 4.9(i), the following conditions are equivalent

  1. \(\chi| \mathbb{F}_q^\times\) is trivial

  2. The product of the \(\chi_i\) is trivial

  3. \(\mathscr{F}(\chi) = \mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i))\) is the inverse image of a (unique) sheaf on \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\).

  4. The inverse image of \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\) on \(\mathbb{G}_m\) (mapped into \(V^\ast\) via the structural morphism \(\mathbb{F}_q \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k\)) is trivial.
(i)\(\Rightarrow\)(ii). We regard \(\chi\) as a character of \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m(\mathbb{F}_q)=k^\times/\mathbb{F}_q^\times\), and we take \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\) on \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\).

(ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iii). Likewise, we regard \((\chi_i)\) as a character of \((V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m)_n\). The uniqueness in (iii) follows from the fact that \(V^\ast\) is a bundle with connected fibres over \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\), and (iii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iv) is trivial.
(iv)\(\Rightarrow\)(i), (ii). This inverse image is \(\mathscr{F}(\chi|\mathbb{F}_q^\times)\) and \(\mathscr{K}_n(\prod \chi_i)\).

Let \(k\) be an étale algebra over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), of dimension \(N+1\) and let \(\chi\) be a non-trivial character of \(k^\times\), trivial on \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\). The Jacobi sum \(J(\chi)\) is defined by
\[ \tag{4.14.1} J(\chi) = (-1)^{N-1} \sum_{\substack{x\in k^\times/\mathbb{F}_q^\times \\ \operatorname{tr}(x)=0}} \chi^{-1}(x) \text{.} \]
Between Gauss sums and Jacobi sums we have the following identity.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.15

For \(\chi\) as above and \(\psi\) a non-trivial additive character of \(\mathbb{F}_q\), we have

\[ q J(\chi) = \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi) \text{.} \]
In the special case where \(k=\mathbb{F}_q^n\), this formula is rewritten by (4.5.3)
\[ \tag{4.15.1} q J(\chi) = \prod_i \tau(\chi_i,\psi) \text{,} \]
or rather written in the form

\begin{align*} \chi_0(-1) J(\chi) &= (-1)^{N-1} \sum_{\substack{x_1,\dots,x_N\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times \\ \sum x_i = 1}} \prod_{i=1}^N \chi_i^{-1}(x_i) = \tau(\chi_0^{-1},\psi)^{-1} \prod_{i=1}^N \tau(\chi_i,\psi) \\ \chi_0^{-1} &= \prod_{i=1}^N \chi_i \end{align*}

blocks.title: Preuve de 4.15
blocks.html:
Proof of 4.15▾
