\[ \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi) = (-1)^{N+1} \sum_{x\in k^\times} \chi(x)^{-1} \psi \operatorname{tr}(x) = (-1)^{N+1} \sum_{x\in k^\times/\mathbb{F}_q^\times} \chi(x)^{-1} \sum_{\lambda\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times} \psi(\lambda \operatorname{tr} x) \text{.} \]

The sum \(\sum_{\lambda\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times} \psi(\lambda \operatorname{tr} x)\) equals \(q-1\) if \(\operatorname{tr}(x)=0\), and \(-1\) if \(\operatorname{tr}(x)\ne 0\). Hence,

\[ \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi) = (-1)^{N+1} \left(q\sum_{x\in k^\times/\mathbb{F}_q^\times} \chi(x)^{-1} - \sum_{x\in k^\times/\mathbb{F}_q^\times} \chi(x)^{-1}\right) \text{.} \]

The second term on the right-hand side is zero, being the sum of the values of a character, and 4.15 follows.

C.Q.F.D.
Proposition 4.15 is thus transposed into cohomology:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.16

The cohomology of \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) (4.6, 4.8) with coefficients in \(\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1})\) satisfies

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i=0\) for \(i\ne N-1\), and \(\dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{N-1}{}=1\).

  2. On \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{N-1}\), \(F^\ast\) is multiplication by \(J(\chi)\).

  3. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{N-1}\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{N+1}\left(V^\ast,\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1},\psi\circ \operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q})\right)(1)\).
Assertion (ii) follows from (i) and the trace formula; (i) and (iii) follow from 4.11 and the following more geometric statement.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.17

Let \((\chi_i)_{i\in I}\) be a family of non-trivial characters of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n(\mathbb{F})\), with product \(1\). Then, \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{i-1}\left(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{K}_m((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\right)\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{i+1}\left(V^\ast,\mathscr{K}_m((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\otimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q})\right)(1)\).
The first line of 4.15 becomes (\(\pi\) as in (4.6.1)).

\[ \tag{4.17.1} \mathsf{R}^i \pi_!\left(\mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\otimes \mathscr{F}(\psi \operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q})\right) = \mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I}) \otimes \mathsf{R}^i \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q}) \]

(on \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\)). Let us compute the sheaves \(\mathsf{R}^i\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\operatorname{tr}_{k/\mathbb{F}_q}) = \mathsf{R}^i \pi_! T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\). Let \(v_0:\widetilde V_0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V_0\) be the blow-up of \(V_0\) at \(\{0\}\). In the diagram
\[ \tag{4.17.2} \xymatrix{ V_0\setminus \{0\} \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[dr]_-\pi & \widetilde V_0 \ar[r]^-{v_0} \ar[d]^-{\overline{\pi}} & V_0 \\ & P_0 } \]

\(\pi\) is a fibration with fibre a punctured line, \(\widetilde V_0\) is the corresponding line bundle, and \(Z_0=v_0^{-1}(0)\) its \(0\)-section. The sheaf \(T^\ast\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(V-0\setminus \{0\}\) extends to \((T v_0)^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(\widetilde V_0\), and the restriction of this sheaf to \(Z_0\) is the constant sheaf \(E_\lambda\), because \(T_0 v_0\) is zero on \(Z_0\). The long exact sequence of cohomology with proper support is therefore written

\[ \tag{4.17.3} \xymatrix{ \ar[r] & \mathsf{R}^i \pi_! T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi) \ar[r] & \mathsf{R}^i \overline{\pi}_! (T v)^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi) \ar[r] & (E_\lambda\text{ for } i=0 \text{, } 0 \text{ otherwise}) \ar[r] & } \]

The inverse image \(\overline{\pi}^{-1}(Q_0)\) is the blow-up \(\widetilde W_0\) of \(W_0\) at \(0\); \(T_0 V_0\) vanishes on \(\widetilde W_0\); we therefore have \((T v)^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)=E_\lambda\) on \(\pi^{-1}(Q_0)\) and, \(\overline{\pi}\) being a line bundle
\[ \tag{4.17.4} \mathsf{R}^i \overline{\pi}_! (T v)^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)|Q = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } i\ne 2 \\ E_\lambda(-1) & \text{for } i=2 \text{.} \end{cases} \]
If \(x\in P\), \(x\notin Q\), the line \(D=\pi^{-1}(x)\) is mapped isomorphically onto \(\mathbb{G}_a\) by \(T v\); we therefore have 2.7*)

\begin{align*} \notag \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(D,(T v)^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)) &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\mathbb{G}_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi)) = 0 && \text{and} \\ \tag{4.17.5} \mathsf{R}^i \overline{\pi}_! (T v)^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi) &= \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } i\ne 2 \\ E_\lambda(-1)_Q & \text{for } i=2 \end{cases} \end{align*}
Combining (4.17.3) and (4.17.5), we finally find
\[ \tag{4.17.6} \mathsf{R}^i \pi_! T^\ast\mathscr{F}(\psi) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } i\ne 1,2 \\ E_\lambda & \text{for } i=1 \\ E_\lambda(-1)_Q & \text{for } i=2 \text{.} \end{cases} \]

Let us compute the cohomology with proper support of the sheaf \(\mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i))\otimes T^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(V^\ast\) by means of the Leray spectral sequence of \(\pi:V^\ast\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\). Applying (4.17.1) and (4.17.6), we find as initial terms the \(E_2^{p,1} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{K}_n(\chi_i)) = 0\) (because \((\chi_i)\ne 0\)) and the \(E_2^{p,2} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{K}(\chi_i))(-1)\).
The spectral sequence reduces to an isomorphism, and 4.17 follows.

The sheaves \(\mathscr{K}_n((\chi_i)_{i\in I})\) make sense over any field, indeed over any base scheme. This will allow us to generalize 4.16(i). With the notation of 4.6, suppose \(M\) finite étale everywhere of rank \(N\) over \(A\), and let \(n\) be an integer invertible in \(A\). We denote by \(a\) the projection of \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) onto \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Let also \(\chi\) be a character (morphism of sheaves) \(\chi:(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m)_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda^\times\), and \(\mathscr{K}_n(\chi)\) the corresponding sheaf. Locally for the étale topology, we may regard \(\chi\) as a family of characters \((\chi_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\), with trivial product.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.20

  1. If \(\chi\) is (at every point) non-trivial, we have \(\mathsf{R}^i a_! (\mathscr{K}_n(\chi)) = 0\) for \(i\ne N-1\), and \(\mathsf{R}^{N-1} a_!(\mathscr{K}_n(\chi))\) is smooth, of rank \(1\).

  2. An automorphism \(\sigma\) of \(M\) that respects \(\chi\) acts on this \(\mathsf{R}^{N-1} a_!\) by multiplication by the signature \(\varepsilon(\sigma)\) of \(\sigma\), viewed as a permutation of \(I\).

  3. If the \(\chi_i\) are all non-trivial, we have \(\mathsf{R} a_! \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R} a_\ast\).

blocks.title: Preuve
blocks.html:
Proof▾

The scheme \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) is the complement of a relative normal crossings divisor in the scheme \(Q\), proper and smooth over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\), and \(\mathscr{K}_n(\chi)\) is locally constant on \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\), with tame ramification at infinity. It follows that the \(\mathsf{R}^i a_!\) and \(\mathsf{R}^i a_\ast\) are smooth, of formation compatible with every base change. A standard argument then reduces us to assuming that \(A\) is a finite field, and (i) follows from 4.17 and 4.11(i). To prove (ii), we use the fact that the action of \(\sigma\) is compatible with the isomorphism 4.17, and 4.12. For (iii), we note that if the \(\chi_i\) are all non-trivial, then \(\mathscr{K}_n(\chi)\) on \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\subset Q\) is ramified along each divisor at infinity, and 1.19.1.

C.Q.F.D.
5 Hecke characters

Let \(F\) be a number field (of finite degree over \(\mathbb{Q}\)) and \(k\) a field of characteristic \(0\). Here are various equivalent ways of saying what an algebraic homomorphism \(\alpha:F^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\) is.
1. Let \(\{e_i\}\) be a basis of \(F\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\). The homomorphism \(\alpha\) is algebraic if it is given by a formula \(\alpha(\sum x^i e_i) = A(x^i)\), \(A\in k(X^i)\).

This means that \(\alpha\) coincides on \(F^\times\) with a rational map defined over \(k\) from \(\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\) to \(\mathbb{G}_m\). By the Zariski density of \(F^\times\), and the fact that a birational homomorphism is everywhere defined, such a map is a homomorphism of group schemes:

1. \(\alpha\) is induced by a homomorphism of \(k\)-group schemes

    \[ \operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\otimes_\mathbb{Q} k \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m \text{.} \]
If \(k\) is a number field, the adjunction property of the restriction of scalars \(R\) shows that this is equivalent to

1. (\(k\) a number field) \(\alpha\) is induced by a homomorphism of \(\mathbb{Q}\)-group schemes: \(\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{R}_{k/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\).

Let \(\overline{k}\) be an algebraic closure of \(k\), and \(I=\hom(F,\overline{k})\). Over \(\overline{k}\), the group of characters of \(\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\) is \(\mathbb{Z}^I\), with basis the embeddings of \(F\) into \(\overline{k}\). The characters defined over \(k\) are those invariant under \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{k}/k)\); they can be described either as those sending \(F^\times\) into \(k^\times\subset \overline{k}\), or in terms of the orbits of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{k}/k)\) in \(I\), themselves corresponding to the factors of \(F\otimes k\).

1. \(\alpha\) is of the form \(\alpha=\prod_{\omega\in I} \omega^{n_\omega}\). The admissible families of exponents \((n_\omega)\) are those such that \(n_\omega=n_{\omega'}\) for \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\) in the same orbit of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{k}/k)\). They are also those such that \(\prod_\omega (x)^{n_\omega}\in k\) for all \(x\in F\).

  2. Set \(F\otimes k=\prod_{j\in J} F_j\), the \(F_j\) being fields. Then \(\alpha\) is written \(\alpha=\prod N_{F_j/k}^{m_j}\).

In the special case where \(k\) contains a normal closure of \(F\), these expressions become: \(\alpha=\prod \omega^{n_\omega}\), where \(\omega\) runs over the \([F:\mathbb{Q}]\) embeddings of \(F\) into \(k\).

Suppose that \(k\) is a number field, and let \(\alpha\) be an algebraic homomorphism from \(F^\times\) to \(k^\times\). Then there exists one and only one homomorphism, again denoted \(\alpha\), from the group \(I(F)\) of fractional ideals of \(F\) to that of \(k\), such that \(\alpha((x))=(\alpha(x))\). Uniqueness follows from the fact that every ideal \(a\) has a power which is a principal ideal, and from the fact that \(I(k)\) is torsion-free. To prove existence, one uses for example 5.1(v): one has \(\alpha(a) = \prod N_{F_j/k}^{m_j}((a))\).

Let us recall the definition of the algebraic Hecke characters, called by Weil Hecke characters (or: grössencharaktere) of type \(A_0\). Let \(F\) be a number field, \(\mathfrak{m}\) an ideal of \(F\) (i.e., of the ring of integers of \(F\)), \(I_\mathfrak{m}\) the group of fractional ideals of \(F\) prime to \(\mathfrak{m}\), and \(k\) a field of characteristic \(0\). A homomorphism \(\chi:I_\mathfrak{m} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\) is an algebraic Hecke character (of conductor \(\leqslant \mathfrak{m}\)) if there exists an algebraic homomorphism \(\chi_\text{alg}:F^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\) satisfying
\[ \tag{*} \text{For } x\in F^\times \text{, prime to } \mathfrak{m} \text{, totally positive and } \equiv 1\pmod\mathfrak{m} \text{, one has } \chi((x))=\chi_\text{alg}(x) \text{.} \]

By the density of the set of \(x\) in (*), \(\chi_\text{alg}\) is entirely determined by \(\chi\). It is the algebraic part of \(\chi\). If \(\chi((x))=\chi_\text{alg}(x)\) for \(x\) totally positive and \(\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{m}'}\), \(\chi\) extends to a Hecke character of conductor \(\leqslant \inf(\mathfrak{m},\mathfrak{m}')\): \(I_{\mathfrak{m}+\mathfrak{m}'}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\). One identifies the Hecke characters that coincide on their common domain of definition, and one calls the conductor of \(\chi\) the smallest \(\mathfrak{m}'\) such that \(\chi\) is of conductor \(\leqslant \mathfrak{m}'\).
5.4 Remark

If an algebraic Hecke character \(\chi\) takes its values in a subfield \(k'\) of \(k\), it is already a Hecke character with values in \(k'\): it suffices to see that \(\chi_\text{alg}:\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m\) is already defined over \(k'\), and this follows from the Zariski density in \(\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\) of the set of \(x\) totally positive \(\equiv 1\pmod\mathfrak{m}\). One can always take for \(k'\) a subfield of \(k\) of finite degree over \(\mathbb{Q}\).

If \(\varepsilon\) is a totally positive unit \(\equiv 1\pmod\mathfrak{m}\), one has \(\chi_\text{alg}(\varepsilon) = \chi((\varepsilon)) = 1\). The homomorphism \(\chi_\text{alg}\) therefore factors through the quotient \(T_\mathfrak{m}\) of \(\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\) by the Zariski closure of the group \(E_\mathfrak{m}\subset F^\times\) of totally positive units \(\equiv 1\pmod\mathfrak{m}\).

According to Serre [35], if \(k\) is an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{Q}\), and \(\mathfrak{m}\) is large enough, the characters \(\prod \omega^{n_\omega}\) of \(\operatorname{R}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_m)\) of the form \(\chi_\text{alg}\) are characterized as follows: there must exist an integer \(N\), the weight of \(\chi\) (or of \(\chi_\text{alg}\)), such that for every element \(\sigma\) of \(\operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbb{Q})\) conjugate to complex conjugation, one has \(n_\omega+n_{\sigma \omega}=N\). If \(F_1\) is the largest subfield of \(F\) which is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field \(F_1'\), this amounts to saying that \(\chi_\text{alg}\) is of the form \(\chi_1\circ N_{F/F_1}\), and that \(\chi_1|F_1=(N_{F_1/\mathbb{Q}})^N\).

If \(\chi\) is of weight \(N\), then for every ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) of \(F\), \(\chi(\mathfrak{a})\) is an algebraic number all of whose conjugates have absolute value \(N(\mathfrak{a})^{N/2}\) [35].
For \(k\) a fixed number field, additional conditions are imposed on \(\chi_\text{alg}\). Indeed, for every ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) of \(F\) prime to the conductor, one has
\[ \tag{5.6.1} \chi_\text{alg}(\mathfrak{a}) = (\chi(\mathfrak{a})) \text{,} \]

so that \(\chi_\text{alg}(\mathfrak{a})\) is principal. Since the group of fractional ideals of \(k\) is torsion-free, it suffices to prove the \(n\)-th power of (5.6.1), for suitable \(n\ne 0\); this allows one to replace \(\mathfrak{a}\) by \(\mathfrak{a}^n\), hence to assume \(\mathfrak{a}=(x)\), with \(x\) totally positive \(\equiv 1\pmod\mathfrak{m}\). It only remains to use the definitions.
This, together with 5.5, shows that \(\chi_\text{alg}\) determines the norm of the \(\chi(\mathfrak{a})\) at all places of \(k\).

Serre's group \(S_\mathfrak{m}\) could be characterized as the group of multiplicative type whose group of characters (over any field) is the group of algebraic Hecke characters of conductor \(\leqslant \mathfrak{m}\). (cf. [35]). Its relation with the \(\ell\)-adic representations is explained in [35].

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.8 ([35])

Let \(\chi\) be an algebraic Hecke character of \(F\) into \(E_\lambda\), for \(E_\lambda\) a finite extension of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\). Then there exists one (and only one) homomorphism \(\chi_\lambda:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\textnormal{ab} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E_\lambda\), such that

  1. \(\chi_\lambda\) is unramified outside the conductor \(\mathfrak{f}\) of \(\chi\) and \(\ell\).

  2. For \(\mathfrak{p}\) a prime ideal of \(F\) prime to \(\mathfrak{f}\) and to \(\ell\), and \(F_\mathfrak{p}\in \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\textnormal{ab}\) the geometric Frobenius at \(\mathfrak{p}\), one has

    \[ \chi_\lambda(F_\mathfrak{p}) = \chi(\mathfrak{p}) \text{.} \]

In the remainder of this section, we shall give a criterion for a \(\lambda\)-adic representation to arise in this way from a Hecke character, and, in the next section, we shall apply it to Jacobi sums. We thus recover, slightly generalized, results of Weil [42, 44], with the second part of Weil's proof replaced by an \(\ell\)-adic cohomology argument.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.10

Let \(F\) and \(k\) be two number fields, \(\lambda\) a place of \(k\) of characteristic \(\ell\), and \(\chi_\lambda:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\textnormal{ab}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k_\lambda^\times\) a homomorphism, unramified outside \(\ell\) and a finite set \(S\) of places. Suppose that there exist a set \(T\) of places (containing \(S\) and the places above \(\ell\)), of density \(0\), and an algebraic homomorphism \(\chi_0:F^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\) such that

  1. For \(\overline{k}\) an algebraic closure of \(k\), \(\chi_0:F^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \hookrightarrow \overline{k}^\times\) is of the type considered in 5.5, of weight \(N\);

  2. For \(\mathfrak{p}\) prime \(\notin T\), \(\chi_\lambda(F_\mathfrak{p})\) is in \(k^\times\), \((\chi_\lambda(F_\mathfrak{p}))=\chi_0(\mathfrak{p})\), and all the complex conjugates of \(\chi_\lambda(F_\mathfrak{p})\) have absolute value \((N \mathfrak{p})^{N/2}\).

Then \(\chi_\lambda\) is defined (5.8) by an algebraic Hecke character of \(F\) with values in \(k\), with algebraic part \(\chi_0\).

Let \(\chi'\) be an algebraic Hecke character with values in a finite Galois extension \(k'\) of \(k\), with algebraic part \(\chi_0\) (5.5). Enlarging \(T\) if necessary, one may assume that the conductor of \(\chi'\) has support in \(T\). Let \(\lambda'\) be a place of \(k'\) above \(\lambda\), \(\chi_{\lambda'}\) the composite \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k_\lambda^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} {k'}_{\lambda'}^\times\), and \(\chi_{\lambda'}':\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} {k'}_{\lambda'}^\times\) defined by \(\chi'\) (5.8). Set \(\varepsilon = \chi_{\lambda'} \cdot {\chi'}_{\lambda'}^{-1}\).

Hypothesis (ii), together with 5.5, 5.6, 5.8, ensure that for \(\mathfrak{p}\notin T\), one has \(\varepsilon(F_\mathfrak{p})\in {k'}^\times\), and that, in all the completions of \(k'\), this number has norm \(1\). It follows that \(\varepsilon(F_\mathfrak{p})\) belongs to the (finite) group \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) of roots of unity of \(k'\). By Cebotarev's density theorem, and the density hypothesis made on \(T\), the \(F_\mathfrak{p}\) (\(\mathfrak{p}\notin T\)) are dense in \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab}\), so that \(\varepsilon(\sigma)\in \mu\) for all \(\sigma\in \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab}\): the character \(\varepsilon\) is a character of finite order \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mu\). By class field theory, it corresponds to a character of finite order of the group of idèle classes of \(F\), i.e. to an algebraic Hecke character with trivial algebraic part. Correcting \(\chi'\) by this character, we reduce to assuming that \(\chi_{\lambda'}=\chi_{\lambda'}'\), and it remains to show that \(\chi'\), a priori with values in \(k'\), in fact has values in \(k\). If \(\sigma\in \operatorname{Gal}(k'/k)\), \(\chi'\) and \({\chi'}^\sigma\) coincide on every prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\notin T\), since \(\chi'(\mathfrak{p}) = \chi'_{\lambda'}(F_\mathfrak{p}) = \chi_{\lambda'}(F_\mathfrak{p}) \in k^\times\). The characters \(\chi_{\lambda'}'\) and \({\chi_{\lambda'}'}^\sigma\) therefore coincide on a dense part of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab}\), hence are equal, so that \(\chi'={\chi'}^\sigma\): \(\chi'\) has values in \(k\).

pages.title: The Hecke characters defined by Jacobi sums

blocks.html: 6 The Hecke characters defined by Jacobi sums

The idea of this section is the following. Consider a Gauss sum \(\tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi)\). It, and the corresponding sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\chi^{-1}\psi)\), are doubly linked to the characteristic \(p\), and to the base field \(\mathbb{F}_q\):

1. because there appears the additive character \(\psi\), and the sheaf \(\sf(\psi)\);

  2. because \(\mathscr{F}(\chi)\) is defined from the Lang exact sequence

    \[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & k^\times \ar[r] & V^\ast \ar[r] & V^\ast \ar[r] & 0 . } \]

Two difficulties if one wants to lift to a number field \(F\) the corresponding cohomological constructions, and to find \(\ell\)-adic representations of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)\) where the eigenvalues of Frobenius are Gauss sums.

If \(\chi\) is trivial on \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\), the sum \(\tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\chi,\psi)\) is independent of \(\psi\), and is \(q\) times a Jacobi sum. The latter is linked to the cohomology of \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\), with values in a sheaf deduced from \(\chi\): \(\psi\), and difficulty a), have disappeared. To resolve b), it suffices to describe the sheaves used by means of Kummer exact sequences (which make sense in every characteristic). This is possible thanks to 4.9.
Once the \(\ell\)-adic representations have been found, one uses 5.10 and Stickelberger's theorem to show that they come from algebraic Hecke characters.

If \(E\) is a field, with algebraic closure \(\overline{E}\), and \(\lambda\) is a character of order dividing \(n\) of \(\mu_d(\overline{E})\), we denote by \(_n\lambda\) the character of \(\mu_n(\overline{E})\) such that \(\lambda\) and \(_n \lambda\) induce the same character of \(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}(1)_{\overline{E}} = \varinjlim \mu_n(\overline{E})\). Likewise for \(\lambda\) a character of \(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}(1)_{\overline{E}}\).

Let \(F\) and \(k\) be two number fields, \(\overline{F}\) an algebraic closure of \(F\), \(I\) a finite set equipped with an action of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)\) and \(\lambda=(\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\) a family of characters \(\lambda_i:\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}(1)_{\overline{F}} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\). Suppose that \(\lambda_i\ne 1\) (\(i\in I\)), that the product of the \(\lambda_i\) is trivial and that the family \(\lambda\) is defined over \(F\), i.e. that for all \(\sigma\in \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)\), one has \(\lambda_{\sigma(i)}=\lambda_i\circ \sigma^{-1}\).

The Galois set \(I\) is the set of homomorphisms into \(\overline{F}\) of an algebra \(E\) separable over \(F\). If \(C\) is the set of orbits of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)\) in \(I\), one has a decomposition of \(E\) into a product of fields \(E=\prod_{\alpha\in C} E_\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is identified with the set of embeddings of \(E_\alpha\) into \(\overline{F}\). If the characters \(\lambda_i\), for \(i\in \alpha\), are of order \(d_\alpha\), the field \(E_\alpha\) contains the \(d_\alpha\)-th roots of \(1\) and there exists \(\lambda_\alpha:\mu_{d_\alpha}(E_\alpha) \hookrightarrow k^\times\) such that, if \(i\in \alpha\) corresponds to the embedding \(\sigma_i\) of \(E_\alpha\) into \(\overline{F}\), one has \(_{d_\alpha} \lambda_i = \lambda_\alpha \sigma_i^{-1}\).

Let \(n>0\) be a multiple of the \(d_\alpha\), \(\Sigma\) the set of places of \(F\) where \(E/F\) ramifies or which divide \(n\), \(\mu\) a place of \(k\) of residue characteristic \(\ell\), and \(A\) the ring of elements of \(F\) integral outside \(\Sigma\) and \(\ell\). The integral closure \(M\) of \(A\) is finite étale of rank \(N=|I|\) over \(A\). With the notations of 4.6, 4.8, the \(_n \lambda_i\) define
\[ _n\lambda:(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m)_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \subset k_\mu^\times \text{.} \]

Let \(a\) be the projection of \(W^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\) onto \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). By 4.20, the sheaf \(\mathsf{R}^{N-2} a_! \mathscr{K}_n(_n \lambda)\) is smooth of rank one; it defines an \(\ell\)-adic representation
\[ j_\mu[\lambda]:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F)^\text{ab} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k_\mu^\times \]
(or simply \(j_\mu\)) unramified outside \(\sigma\) and \(\ell\).

Let us compute \(j_\mu(F_\mathfrak{p})\). By 4.20, it suffices to do so after reduction modulo \(\mathfrak{p}\). So let \(f=A/\mathfrak{p}\), \(e=M/\mathfrak{p} M\), and \(\overline{f}\) the algebraic closure of \(f\) defined by a place of \(\overline{F}\) above \(\mathfrak{p}\). One still has \(I=\hom_f(e,\overline{f})\). After reduction, \(_n\lambda\) still admits a description 6.1:

1. Let \(D\) be the set of orbits of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{f}/f)\) in \(I\). The decomposition of \(e\) into a product of fields is written \(e=\prod_{\beta\in D} e_\beta\), where the \(\sigma_i\) (\(i\in \beta\)) are identified with the embeddings of \(e_\beta\) into \(F\). For \(\beta\in D\), we denote by \(\alpha(\beta)\) the element of \(C\) containing \(\beta\) and \(d_\beta=d_{\alpha(\beta)}\). Let

    \[ \xymatrix{ \lambda_\beta : \mu_{d_\beta}(e_\beta) & \mu_{d_\beta}(E_{\alpha(\beta)}) \ar[r]^-{\lambda_{d(\beta)}} \ar[l]_-\sim& k^\times . } \]

  2. If \(i\in I\) corresponds to the embedding \(\sigma_i\) of \(e_\beta\) into \(\overline{f}\), the reduction \(_{d\beta} \overline{\lambda}_i:\mu_{d\beta}(\overline{f}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\) of \(_{d\beta} \lambda_i\) of \(_{d\beta} \lambda_i\) is \(\lambda_\beta \circ \sigma_i^{-1}\).

Let \(q_\beta\) be the number of elements of \(e_\beta\), \(\chi_\beta=_{(q_{\beta^{-1}})} \lambda_\beta\), and \(\chi:e^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\) with coordinates the \(\chi_\beta\). On the affine space over \(A/\mathfrak{p}\) defined by \(e\) (4.6), or rather on the torus \(e_\beta^\times\), one has isomorphisms \(\mathscr{K}_n((_n\overline{\lambda}_i)_{i\in\beta}) = \mathscr{K}_{d_\beta}((\lambda_\beta \circ \sigma_i^{-1})_{i\in\beta}) =\mathscr{K}_{q_{\beta^{-1}}}((\chi_\beta\circ \sigma_i^{-1})_{i\in I}) = \mathscr{F}(\chi_\beta)\) (4.9). On \(e^\times\), one thus has \(\mathscr{K}_n((_n\overline{\lambda}_i)_{i\in \beta}) = \mathscr{F}(\chi)\) and this isomorphism descends to the reduction mod \(\mathfrak{p}\) of \(V^\ast/\mathbb{G}_m\). Hence

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4

With the notations of 6.2 and 6.3, \(j_\mu(F_\mathfrak{p})\) is the Jacobi sum \(J(\chi)\).
Let us rewrite the formulas linking \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\) to \((\chi_\beta)_{\beta\in B}\): for \(i\in \beta\subset \alpha\),

\begin{align*} _{d_\alpha} \lambda_i &= \lambda_\alpha\circ \sigma_i^{-1} && \lambda_\alpha:\mu_{d_\alpha}(E_\alpha) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \\ \lambda_\beta &= \text{reduction of } \lambda_\alpha && :\mu_{d_\alpha}(e_\beta) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \\ \chi_\beta &= _{q_{\beta^{-1}}}\lambda_\beta: x\mapsto \lambda_\beta(x^{(q_\beta-1)/d_\alpha}) && :e_\beta^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times \end{align*}

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.5

The representation \(j_\mu\) is defined by an algebraic Hecke character of \(F\) with values in \(k^\times\).
We shall verify this by means of 5.10. Here we rejoin Weil's proof [42, 44], through the use of Stickelberger's theorem, and I shall give only a few indications.

Given \(j:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k_\lambda^\times\), and a finite extension \(F'/F\), one verifies by means of 5.10 that \(j\) is defined by a Hecke character if and only if \(j|\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F')\) is. This remark allows one in 6.5 to reduce to the case where Galois acts trivially on \(I\), and where \(F\) contains the \(n\)-th roots of unity. One can then reduce to the case where \(F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\), and then take \(k=F\). In this case, each \(_n \lambda_i\) is defined by \(a_i\in \mathbb{Z}/n\): it is \(x\mapsto x^{a_i}:\mu_n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k^\times\). One has \(\sum a_i=0\), and \(a_i\ne 0\).

In a number field, the places of degree \(1\) always form a set of density \(0\). By applying 5.10, one may therefore neglect the others, and use Stickelberger only for a prime field. So let \(p\) be prime, \(0<a<p-1\), \(\widetilde x:\mathbb{F}_p^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Q}_p^\times\) the “multiplicative lift” character and \(g=-\sum_{x\in \mathbb{F}_p^\times} \widetilde x^{-a} \zeta^z\in \mathbb{Q}_p(\zeta)\), for \(\zeta\) a \(p\)-th root of \(1\). Denote again by \(x\) the integer in \([0,p-1]\) lifting \(x\), and expand \(\zeta^x=(1+\pi)x\) by the binomial formula. One finds \(g=-\sum_{0=0}^{p-1} A_i\pi^i\) with \(A_i\in \mathbb{Z}_p\), whose reduction \(\mod p\) is the sum \(\sum_{x\in \mathbb{F}_p^\times} x^{-a} \binom x i\). For \(b\) not divisible by \(p-1\), one has \(\sum_{x\in \mathbb{F}_p^\times} x^b=0\). If \(i<a\), \(\binom x i\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(i<a\), whence \(A_i\equiv 0\pmod p\). Similarly, \(A_a\equiv \frac{p-1}{a!} \pmod p\), and \(g\sim \frac{\pi^a}{a!}\): the valuation of \(g\) is given by \(v(g)/v(p) = \frac{a}{p-1}\).

Let \(\sigma_i\) (\(i\in (\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\)) be the element of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})/\mathbb{Q})\) such that \(\sigma_i(\zeta)=\zeta^i\) for \(\zeta^n=1\), and let us denote additively the group of algebraic homomorphisms \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})^\times \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})^\times\). For \(\lambda\) as in 6.6, defined by a family \((a_i)_{i\in I}\) of integers \(\mod n\), nonzero and of sum zero 5.10, (4.15.1) and 6.7 show that \(j_\mu[\lambda]\) is defined by an algebraic Hecke character \(j[a]\) and that, if \(N\) is the norm, its algebraic part is given by
\[ \tag{6.8.1} (N j[a])_\text{alg} = \sum_{i\in (\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times} \sum_{j\in I} \left \lfloor \frac{i a_j}{n} \right\rfloor \sigma_i^{-1} \]
where \(\lfloor \cdot \rfloor\) is the fractional part.
The most interesting case is that where \(F\subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\), and where the family of the \(_n \lambda_i\) is constructed as follows:

1. One takes a finite family \((Aj)_{j\in J}\) of orbits of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\sqrt[n]{1}/F)=H\subset (\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\) in \(\mathbb{Z}/n\). One assumes that \(A_j\ne\{0\}\) and that \(\sum_{j\in J} \sum_{a\in A_j} a=0\).

  2. One takes \(I=\sqcup_{j\in J} A_j\); Galois acts on each \(A_j\).

  3. One takes \(\overline{F}\supset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\), \(k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\) and, if \(i\in I\) corresponds to \(a\in A_j\subset (\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\), \(_n\lambda_i(x)=x^a\).

One verifies by means of 4.20 that a general \(j_\mu\) (relative to \(F_1\)) is deduced from a \(j_\mu\) as above (for \(F\subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\), \(F_1\) an extension of \(F\)) by restriction to \(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{F}/F_1)\) and multiplication by a character of order two.

For \(a\in \operatorname{Gal}(k/\mathbb{Q})=(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\), \(a\) transforms the family of the \(A_j\) into that of the \(a A_j\). If \(a\in H\), the family of the \(A_j\) is therefore preserved, and the \(j_\mu(F_\mathfrak{p})\) are invariant under \(H\):

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.10

Under the hypotheses of 6.9, \(j_\mu\) is defined by an algebraic Hecke character of \(F\) with values in \(F\).

Let us again take \(F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\), and consider the Hecke characters \(j[a]\) defined by a family \((a_i)_{i\in I}\), \(i\in \mathbb{Z}/n\), \(a_i\ne 0\), \(\sum a_i=0\). The following theorem was obtained independently by Vishik.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.11

Every algebraic Hecke character of \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{1})\), \(a\), has a power in the group generated by the \(j[a]\) and the norm.

Since one works “up to torsion,” only the algebraic part of the Hecke characters considered matters. Applying (6.8.1) to the \(j[a]\), with \(a=\) an element of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) repeated \(n\) times, one reduces to the following lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.12

Denote by \(\sum x_j \sigma_j\) the elements of the group algebra \(\mathbb{Q}[(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times]\), and let \(x\) be the subgroup of those such that \(x_j+x_{-j}=C^{\underline{t e}}\). Then \(X\) is generated over \(\mathbb{Q}\) by \(N=\sum \sigma_j\) and by the \(g_a=\sum \left\lfloor \frac{i a}{n}\right\rfloor \sigma)i^{-1}\) (\(a\in \mathbb{Z}/n\), \(a\ne 0\)).

Both \(X\) and \(Y=\langle N,(g_a)\rangle\) are ideals of the group algebra, and it suffices to check that they are annihilated by the same complex characters \(\chi\) of \((\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\). This amounts to saying that an odd character \((\chi(j)=-\chi(-j)\)) never annihilates all the \(g_a\). If \(\chi\) is primitive, one has
\[ \chi(g_1) = \sum \frac i n \chi^{-1}(i) = -L(\chi,0)\ne 0 \text{.} \]
In the general case, if \(\chi\) comes from a primitive character of \((\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\), \(\chi(g_{n/d})\) reduces to an analogous sum over \((\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times\), whence the lemma.
7 Generalized Kloosterman sums
Let \(\mathbb{F}_q\) be a finite field with \(q\) elements, and \(\psi\) a nontrivial additive character. In this section, we make a cohomological study of the generalized Kloosterman sums
\[ \tag{7.1.1} \mathrm{K}_{n,a} = \sum_{x_1\dotsm x_n = a} \psi(x_1+\cdots + x_n) \qquad (n\geqslant 1) \text{.} \]
For \(a=0\), this sum is elementary (cf. 7.7):
\[ \tag{7.1.2} \mathrm{K}_{n,0} = (-1)^{n-1} \text{.} \]
The interesting case is that where \(a\ne 0\). The \(x_i\) are then in \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\). In this case we shall prove an upper bound
\[ \tag{7.1.3} \left|K_{n,a}\right| \leqslant n q^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \text{.} \]
Our essential tools will be the cohomological statements reflected in the following identities

\begin{align*} \tag{7.1.4} \mathrm{K}_{n,a} &= \sum_{x_1} \psi(x_i) \sum_{x_2\dotsm x_n = a/x_1} \psi(x_2+\cdots + x_n) \\ \notag &= \sum_{x\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times} \psi(x) \mathrm{K}_{n-1,a/x} \qquad (a\ne 0,n\geqslant 2) \\ \tag{7.1.5} \sum_a \mathrm{K}_{n,a} &= \sum_a \sum_{x_1 \dotsm x_n = a} \psi\left(\sum x_i\right) = \sum_{x_1,\dots,x_n} \psi\left(\sum x_i\right) = 0 \end{align*}
For \(\chi\) a nontrivial character of \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\),
\[ \tag{7.1.6} \sum \chi(a) \mathrm{K}_{n,a} = \sum_{x_1,\dots,x_n} \chi\left(\prod x_i\right) \cdot \psi\left(\sum x_i\right) = (-\tau(\chi^{-1},\psi))^n \]
(Gauss sum).
Let \(k\) be an étale algebra of degree \(n\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(\varepsilon(k)\) as in (4.5.1). Set
\[ \mathrm{K}_{k,a} = \sum_{N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q}(x)=a} \psi \operatorname{tr}(x) \text{.} \]
One still has

\begin{align*} \tag{7.2.1} \mathrm{K}_{k,0} &= (-1)^{n-1} \cdot \varepsilon(k) \\ \tag{7.2.2} \sum_a \mathrm{K}_{k,a} &= 0 \\ \tag{7.2.3} \sum_a \chi(a) \mathrm{K}_{k,a} &= (-1)^n \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}\left(\chi^{-1}\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\right) \text{.} \end{align*}
By Fourier inversion on \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\), one deduces from it an expression of \(\mathrm{K}_{k,a}\) in terms of Gauss sums:

\begin{align*} \mathrm{K}_{k,a} &= \frac{1}{q-1} \sum_\chi \chi(a) \sum_{b\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times} \chi^{-1}(b) \mathrm{K}_{k,b} \\ \tag{7.2.4} (-1)^n \mathrm{K}_{k,a} &= \frac{1}{q-1} \left(\varepsilon(k) + \sum_{\chi\ne 1} \chi(a) \tau_{\mathbb{F}_q}\left(\chi\circ N_{k/\mathbb{F}_q},\psi\right) \right) \text{.} \end{align*}
The Hasse-Davenport identity now allows one to compare \(\mathrm{K}_{k,a}\) to \(\mathrm{K}_{n,a} = \mathrm{K}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^n},a}\):
\[ \tag{7.2.5} \mathrm{K}_{k,a} = \varepsilon(k) \mathrm{K}_{n,a} \text{.} \]
I do not know a cohomological interpretation of (7.2.4), but I shall give one of (7.2.5). Let us return to the sums \(\mathrm{K}_{n,a}\).

Let \(\mathbb{F}\) be an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{F}_q\) and, for \(a\in \mathbb{F}\), let \(V_a^{n-1}\), or simply \(V_a\), be the hypersurface of \(\mathbb{A}^n\) with equation \(x_1 \dotsm x_n=a\). As usual, we shall regard \(\psi\) as taking \(\ell\)-adic rather than complex values. With the notation 1.8(ii), (7.1.3) is deduced from the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.4

The cohomology of \(V_a^{n-1}\) with values in \(\mathscr{F}(\psi(\sum x_i))\) satisfies

  1. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i=0\) for \(i\ne n-1\);

  2. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet{} \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet{}\);

  3. for \(a\ne 0\), \(\dim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}{}=n\);

  4. for \(a=0\), \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}{}\) is canonically isomorphic to \(E_\lambda\).

As usual, this theorem also controls the dependence of \(\mathrm{K}_{n,a}\) on \(q\): for each \(a\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times\), there exist \(n\) eigenvalues of Frobenius \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\), of complex absolute value \(q^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\), such that
\[ \sum_{\substack{x_1\dotsm x_n = a \\ x_i\in \mathbb{F}_{q^m}}} \psi\circ \operatorname{tr}\left(\sum x_i\right) = (-1)^{n-1} \left(\alpha_1^m + \cdots + \alpha_n^m \right) \text{.} \]

For \(n\) even, \(x\mapsto -x\) is an involution of \(V_a\), which transforms \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) into its dual. Reasoning as in 3.6, one deduces from it a canonical non-degenerate alternating form on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi))\), with values in \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell(-(n-1))\) and the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.6

With the notations of 7.5, if \(n\) is even, the \(\alpha_i\) group into \(\frac n 2\) pairs of roots \(\alpha,\overline{\alpha}\) with product equal to \(q^{n-1}\).

Let us verify the case \(a=0\) of 7.5. The hypersurface \(V_0\) is the union of the coordinate hyperplanes \(x_i=0\). Let us compute the Leray spectral sequence (2.6.1*) of this covering of \(V_0\), for the cohomology with or without support with coefficients in \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\). By 2.7*, all the initial terms vanish, except the cohomology of the intersection \(\{0\}\) of all the coordinate hyperplanes. There remains an isomorphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^0{}\xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0{}=E_\lambda\) which justifies 7.4.

We shall prove 7.4 and 7.8 below by a simultaneous induction on \(n\), relying on the spectral sequence of which (7.1.4) is the reflection. This requires a control of the dependence on \(a\) of \(\mathrm{K}_{n,a}\).

Let \(\pi:\mathbb{A}^n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}\) be the map “product of the coordinates,” and \(\sigma\) the sum of the coordinates. The hypersurfaces \(V_a\) are the fibres of \(\pi\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.8

  1. The sheaf \(\mathsf{R}^{n-1}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) is smooth of rank \(n\) on \(\mathbb{A}^1\setminus \{0\}\).

  2. its extension by \(0\) to \(\mathbb{P}^1\) is the direct image of its restriction to \(\mathbb{A}^1\setminus \{0\}\).

  3. at \(0\), the monodromy is unipotent, with a single Jordan block

  4. at \(\infty\), the wild inertia acts without fixed point \(\ne 0\), and the Swan conductor equals \(1\),

  5. one has \(\mathsf{R}^i \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^i \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) (zero for \(i\ne n-1\)).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Proof▾

that 7.4 (for a given value of \(n\)) implies 7.8 (for the same value of \(n\)).

The fibre of \(\mathsf{R}^i \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) at \(a\) is \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\), and on the dense open set \(\mathbb{A}^1\) where the \(\mathsf{R}^i \pi_!\mathscr{F}(\psi^{-1}\sigma)\) are locally constant that of \(\mathsf{R}^i \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) is \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) ([VII]Th. Finitude 2.1). The hypothesis 7.4(\(n\)) thus provides us with the

Lemma 7.9

  1. \(\mathsf{R}^i \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)=0\) for \(i\ne n-1\).

  2. For \(i=n-1\), the fibre of this sheaf at every point \(a\ne 0\) is of constant rank \(n\). At \(0\), it is of rank \(1\).

  3. On a dense open set \(U\), one has \(\mathsf{R}^i \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^i \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi)\).

We shall now use the Leray spectral sequence of \(\pi\), for cohomology with or without support, with coefficients in \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\). The abutment is known: \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^n,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^n,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = 0\) (2.7*). In cohomology with proper support, 7.9(i) ensures that \(E_2^{pq}=0\) for \(q\ne n-1\). The \(E_2\) terms are therefore all zero:

\[ \tag{7.10.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(\mathbb{A}^1,\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_!\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = 0 \text{.} \]

For \(p=0\), this means that \(\mathsf{R}^{n-1}\pi+! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) has no section with punctual support. In view of the constancy of rank 7.9(ii), we deduce

\[ \tag{7.10.2} \begin{array}{c} \text{The sheaf } \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \text{ on } \mathbb{A}^1 \text{ is smooth on } \mathbb{A}^1\setminus \{0\} \text{, and is } \\ \text{a subsheaf of the direct image } \mathscr{G} \text{ of its restriction to } \mathbb{A}^1\setminus \{0\} \text{.} \end{array} \]

The long exact cohomology sequence of

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & \mathscr{Q} \ar[r] & 0 . } \]

where the support of \(\mathscr{Q}\) is concentrated at \(0\), gives

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^0(\mathbb{A}^1,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & \mathscr{Q}_0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{A}^1,\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) . } \]

The extreme terms being zero, \(\mathscr{Q}=0\) and

\[ \tag{7.10.3} \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \text{ is the direct image of its restriction to } \mathbb{A}^1\setminus \{0\} \text{.} \]

Let \(j\) be the inclusion of \(\mathbb{A}^1\) into \(\mathbb{P}^1\). The “derived category” version of the Leray spectral sequences is

\begin{align*} \mathsf{H}^\bullet(\mathbb{P}^1,j_! \mathsf{R}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) &= \mathsf{H}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^1,\mathsf{R} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^n,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = 0 \\ \mathsf{H}^\bullet(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathsf{R} \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) &= \mathsf{H}^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^1,\mathsf{R} \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\mathbb{A}^n,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = 0 \text{.} \end{align*}

Let \(\Delta\) be the mapping cylinder of \(j_! \mathsf{R}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathsf{R} \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\). By 7.9(iii), the cohomology sheaves of this complex of sheaves have finite support. On the other hand, the long exact cohomology sequence of the triangle \((j_!\mathsf{R} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma),\mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathsf{R} \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma),\Delta)\) shows that \(\mathsf{H}^\bullet(\mathbb{P}^1,\Delta)=0\). One has \(\mathsf{H}^\bullet(\mathbb{P}^1,\Delta) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathscr{H}^\bullet(\Delta))\), and finally \(\Delta=0\):

\[ \xymatrix{ j_! \mathsf{R}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathsf{R} \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) . } \]

In particular, \(\mathsf{R}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}\pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) and, these complexes of sheaves having only one nonzero cohomology sheaf,

\[ \tag{7.10.4} \xymatrix{ j_! \mathsf{R} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \ar[r]^-\sim & j_\ast \mathsf{R} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) . } \]

This completes the proof of (i) (ii) (v).

Let \(\operatorname{Sw}_0\) and \(\operatorname{Sw}_\infty\) be the Swan conductors at \(0\) and at \(\infty\) of \(\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\). One has \(\chi_c(\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))=0\) (7.10.1) and the Euler-Poincaré formula (3.2.1) reduces to

\[ \tag{7.11.1} \operatorname{Sw}_0 + \operatorname{Sw}_\infty =1 \text{:} \]

one of these conductors equals \(0\) (tame ramification), the other equals \(1\).

Let \(\mathscr{G}\) be a sheaf of rank \(1\) on \(\mathbb{G}_m\), of Kummer type 4.7 (\(\mathscr{G}=\mathscr{K}_n(\chi)\)) and non-constant (\(\chi\ne 1\)). The sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\otimes \pi^\ast \mathscr{G}\) on \(V^\ast=\pi^{-1}(\mathbb{G}_m) = \mathbb{A}^n\setminus \pi^{-1}(0)\) is then of the type encountered in the study of Gauss sums, and 4.11(ii) gives us

\[ \tag{7.12.1} \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(V^\ast,\pi^\ast\mathscr{G}\otimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \ar[r]^-\sim & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(V^\ast,\pi^\ast \mathscr{G}\otimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) . } \]

The Leray spectral sequence of \(\pi\) transforms this statement into

\[ \tag{7.12.2} \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{G}\otimes \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \ar[r]^-\sim & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{G}\otimes \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) . } \]

Let \(i\) be the inclusion of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) into \(\mathbb{P}^1\), and \(\Delta\) the mapping cylinder of \(\delta:i_!(\mathscr{G}\otimes \mathsf{R}^{n-1}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi))\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{R} i_\ast (\mathscr{G}\otimes \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) (where \(\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! = \mathsf{R}^{n-1}\pi_\ast\)). Reasoning as in 7.10, we deduce from (7.12.2) that \(\Delta=0\). In particular

\[ \tag{7.12.3} \text{At } 0 \text{ and at } \infty \text{, the inertia acts without fixed point } \ne 0 \text{ on } \mathscr{G}\otimes \mathsf{R}^{n-1}\pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \text{.} \]

At \(\infty\), this holds even if \(\mathscr{G}\) is trivial (7.10.4), so that the wild inertia acts without fixed point. In particular, the ramification is wild: by 7.11, one has \(\operatorname{Sw}_\infty=1\), and the ramification at \(0\) is tame.

At \(0\), (7.12.3) forces the ramification – tame – of \(\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) to be unipotent. By (7.10.3) and 7.9(ii), there is a single Jordan block. This completes the proof of 7.8(\(n\)).

For \(n=1\), 7.4 is trivial. To complete the proof of 7.4 and 7.8, it remains for us to prove that 7.8, for a given value of \(n\), implies 7.4, for \(n+1\). The case \(a=0\) having been treated (7.7), we assume that \(a=0\). We shall write \(x_0,\dots,x_n\) for the coordinates of \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}\). Let \(g=x_0:V_a\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{G}_m\), let \(\tau\) be the involution \(x\mapsto a x^{-1}\) of \(\mathbb{G}_m\), and, as above, let \(\pi\) be the product of the coordinates: \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{A}^1\), and \(\sigma\) their sum. We shall denote by \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) the sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi(\sum x_i))\) both on \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}\) and on \(\mathbb{A}^n\).

Let us write the Leray spectral sequence of \(g\). Since the sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) on \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}\) is the external tensor product of the sheaves \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(\mathbb{A}^1\) and \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) on \(\mathbb{A}^n\), one finds (cf. (7.1.4)).

\begin{align*} 'E_2^{p q} &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi)\otimes \tau^\ast \mathsf{R}^q \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \\ ''E_2^{p q} &= \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi)\otimes \tau^\ast \mathsf{R}^q \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \text{.} \end{align*}

By hypothesis, \(\mathsf{R}^q \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^q \pi_\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\), and this sheaf is zero for \(q\ne n-1\). The sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(\mathbb{G}_m\) is wildly ramified at \(\infty\) and unramified at \(0\), whereas \(\tau^\ast \mathsf{R}^q \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) is wildly ramified at \(0\) (without invariant under the wild inertia, with Swan conductor \(1\)) and tamely ramified at \(\infty\). Their tensor product is therefore

  1. wildly ramified at \(0\) and \(\infty\), without invariant under the wild inertia;

  2. with Swan conductor \(1\) at \(0\) and \(n\) (the rank of \(\mathsf{R}^q \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi))\) at \(\infty\).

One has \('E_2^{p q} \xrightarrow{\sim} ''E_2^{p q}\), and \('E_2^{p q}=0\) except for \(p=1\) and \(q=n-1\). The Euler-Poincaré formula finally gives

\[ \dim{'E_2^{p q}} = 1+n \text{;} \]

this completes the proof.

Q.E.D.
The isomorphism obtained in 7.14

\[ \tag{7.15.1} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^n(V_a^n,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathscr{F}(\psi)\otimes \tau^\ast \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \]

allows, with the notation of 7.5, the computation of the product \(\det(F)\) of the eigenvalues \(\alpha_i\) of Frobenius. The formalism of [13] applies, since \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) and \(\mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\) belong to infinite compatible systems of \(\ell\)-adic representations. This reduces us to local problems, which can be simplified by noting that (cf. [13])

1. the global constants for \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) and \(\tau^\ast \mathsf{R}^{n-1} \pi_! \mathscr{F}(\psi)\) are easy to compute, the cohomology of these sheaves being of trivial nature.

  2. at every point, for either of these sheaves, the corresponding \(\ell\)-adic representation of the decomposition group has an unramified semisimplification.
The result, for the sum in \(n\) variables, is that
\[ \tag{7.15.2} \det\left(F,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a^{n-1},\mathscr{F}(\psi))\right) = q^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}} \text{.} \]

For \(p=2\), the sheaf \(\sf(\psi)\) is orthogonal. For \(a\ne 0\) and \(n\) odd, one deduces from it, by 7.4(ii) and Poincaré duality, a symmetric bilinear form on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a^{n-1},\mathscr{F}(\psi))\), with values in \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(1-n)\). Relative to this form, \(F\) is an orthogonal similitude with multiplier \(q^{n-1}\), and \(q^{\frac{1-n}{2}} F\) belongs to the special orthogonal group, by (7.15.2). One of the eigenvalues of \(F\) is therefore \(q^{\frac{1-n}{2}}\), and the others fall into pairs of roots \(\alpha\), \(\overline{\alpha}\) with product \(q^{n-1}\).
For \(n=3\), L. Carlitz [8] obtained a more precise result, equivalent to the following proposition.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.17

For \(p=2\), and \(\psi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_q}(x)}\), one has an isomorphism

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(V_a^2,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = \operatorname{Sym}^2 \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(V_a^1,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) \text{.} \]

The second tensor power of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(V_a^1,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) is \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(V_a^1\times V_a^1,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\boxtimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) (Künneth), the symmetry \(x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x\) being represented geometrically as \(-\tau^\ast\), where \(\tau\) is the automorphism \((x,y)\mapsto (y,x)\) of \(V_a\times V_a\). If \(X'\) is the quotient of \(V_a^1\times V_a^1\) by \(\{\operatorname{id}{},\tau\}\) and \(\pi\) is the projection of \(V_a^1\times V_a^1\) onto \(X'\), the group \(\operatorname{Sym}^2 \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(V_a^1,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) is therefore identified with the cohomology of \(X'\) with coefficients in the part of \(\pi_\ast(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\boxtimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) anti-invariant under \(\tau\). Let us denote by \(s\) the function on \(X'\) such that \(s\pi =\sigma\mathrm{pr}_1+\sigma\mathrm{pr}_2\). One has \(\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\boxtimes \mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma) = \mathscr{F}(\psi(\sigma\mathrm{pr}_1+\sigma\mathrm{pr}_2)) = \mathscr{F}(\psi s \pi) = \pi^\ast \mathscr{F}(\psi s)\) (isomorphism compatible with \(\tau\)). On the image \(\pi(\Delta)\) of the diagonal, the sheaf of anti-invariants sought is therefore zero, whereas on the complement \(X=X'\setminus \pi(\Delta)\), it is the tensor product of \(\mathscr{F}(\psi s)\) by \(\varepsilon(P)\), for \(\varepsilon\) the unique character of order \(2\) of \(\{1,\tau\}\), and \(P\) the \(\{1,\tau\}\)-torsor on \(X\) that is the double covering induced by \(V_a^1\times V_a^1\). One has
\[ \tag{7.17.1} \operatorname{Sym}^2 \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(V_a^1,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma)\otimes \varepsilon(P)) \text{.} \]

Let us compute \(X\), \(s\) and \(\varepsilon(P)\). On \(V_a^1\times V_a^1\), set \(x_1=x_1\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\), \(x_2=x_2\circ\mathrm{pr}_2\), \(x_1'=x_1\circ \mathrm{pr}_2\), \(x_2'=x_2\circ \mathrm{pr}_2\). One has \(x_1 x_2=x_1'x_2'=a\). Let us identify functions on \(X'\) with functions on \(X\) invariant under \(\tau\). Let \(s_1=x_1+x_1'\), \(s_2=x_2+x_2'\), \(p_1=x_1 x_1'\), \(p_2=x_2 x_2'\). One has \(s_1 p_2 = a s_2\), \(s_2 p_1 = a s_1\) and \(X\) is defined in \(X'\) by \(s_1\ne 0\), \(s_2\ne 0\). On \(X\), one therefore has \(p_1 = a s_1 s_2^{-1}\), and \((s_1,s_2)\) identifies \(x\) with \(\mathbb{G}_m\times \mathbb{G}_m\). On \(X\), the covering \(P\) has equation \(T^2-s_1 T+a s_1 s_2^{-1}\) (take for \(T\) the coordinate \(x_1\)). If \(T=s_1 t\), this rewrites as \(t^2-t+a s_1^{-1} s_2^{-1}\). One therefore has \(\varepsilon(P) = \mathscr{F}(\psi(a s_1^{-1} s_2^{-1}))\). Since \(s=s_1+s-2\), one has \(\mathscr{F}(\psi s)\otimes \varepsilon(P) = \mathscr{F}(\psi(s_1+s_2+ a s_1^{-1} s_2^{-1}))\) and the right-hand side of (7.17.1) is identified with the left-hand side of 7.17.
Remark
\(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(V_a^1,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) is also the first cohomology group of the elliptic curve obtained by completing the affine curve with equation
\begin{align*} y^2-y &= x_1+x_2 \\ x_1 x_2 &= a \text{;} \end{align*}
its modular invariant is \(j=a^{-2}\).
For \(\chi\) a multiplicative character of \(\mathbb{F}_q^\times\), and \(a\ne 0\), the method of 7.14 applies to the study of the sum
\[ s = \sum_{x_0\dotsm x_n = a} \chi(x_0) \psi(x_0+\cdots + x_n) \]

(replace the sheaf \(\mathscr{F}(\psi)\) on \(\mathbb{G}_m\) by \(\mathscr{F}(\chi\cdot \psi)\)). One again finds a cohomology of dimension \(n+1\), and \(|S|\leqslant (n+1)q^{n/2}\). Such sums have been considered by Salie and Mordell [28].
One may hope that our methods allow the study of the sums
\[ S_{k,\chi,a} = \sum_{N(x)=a} \chi(x) \psi \operatorname{tr}(x) \]
(\(k\) an étale algebra over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(a\in \mathbb{F}_q^\times\), \(\chi\) a character of \(k^\times\)). The analogue of 7.4 (for \(a\ne 0\)) should be true.

The symmetric group \(S_n\) acts on \(\mathbb{A}^n\) respecting \(V_a\) and the map \(\sigma\), hence also the sheaf \(\sf(\psi\sigma)\), the inverse image under \(\sigma\) of the sheaf \(\sf(\psi)\) on \(\mathbb{G}_a\). It therefore acts on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\). The formula (7.2.5) admits the following cohomological interpretation

Proposition 7.20

The action of \(S_n\) on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\) is multiplication by the sign character.

This amounts to showing that a transposition \(\tau\) acts by multiplication by \(-1\). Since \(\tau^2=1\), \(\tau\) can only have \(\pm 1\) as eigenvalues. Let \(V_a/\tau\) be the quotient of \(V_a\) for \(\{\operatorname{id},\tau\}\). The map \(\sigma\), hence the sheaf \(\sf(\psi\sigma)\), pass to the quotient, and the subspace of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi))\) fixed by \(\tau\) is \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{n-1}(V_a/\tau,\mathscr{F}(\psi\sigma))\). We must prove that this cohomology is zero.

Suppose that \(a\ne 0\). For \(\tau=(1,2)\) the quotient \(V_a/\tau\) is identified with \(\mathbb{G}_a\times \mathbb{G}_m^{n-2}\), the quotient map being \((x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots,x_n)\mapsto (x_1+x_2,x_3,\dots,x_n)\). Indeed, \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are determined up to order by \(x_1+x_2\) and \(x_1x_2 = a/x_3\dotsm x_n\). In these coordinates \((t,x_3,\dots,x_n)\), the sheaf is written \(\mathscr{F}(\psi(t+x_3+\cdots + x_n)) = \mathscr{F}(\psi(t))\otimes \mathscr{F}(\psi(x_3+\cdots + x_n))\). The Künneth formula, and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_0^\bullet(\mathbb{G}_a,\mathscr{F}(\psi)) = 0\), therefore provide the required vanishing.
For \(a=0\), one can deduce 7.20 from the computation 7.7.

The sums \(\mathrm{K}_{n,a}\) of this section have been studied by S. Sperber, in his thesis, and in [38] by \(p\)-adic methods inspired by Dwork and by Bombieri's article [6]. For \(p\ne 2\), these methods give him the dependence on \(q\) 7.5, the functional equation \(\alpha_i = q^{n-1} \beta_i^{-1}\) between the eigenvalues of Frobenius for the sums \(\mathrm{K}_{n,a}\) and \(\mathrm{K}_{n,b}\) if \(b=(-1)^n a\) (cf. 7.6), and the value 7.15 of the product of the roots. For \(p\geqslant n+3\), he moreover determines the \(p\)-adic valuations of the roots. The result is very beautiful: if the roots \(\alpha_i\) are arranged in a suitable order, with \(0\leqslant i\leqslant n\), the \(\alpha_i q^{-i}\) are units. The restrictions on \(p\) are doubtless not essential.
8 Other applications

The identity 1.9.4 can sometimes be used to compute the number of rational points of an algebraic variety over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). In most cases where an exact result has been obtained, the cohomology is expressed in terms of algebraic cycles; such is the case for rational surfaces, quadrics, smooth intersections of two quadrics of odd dimension, flag varieties…. This is however not always the case; in Lusztig's very beautiful article [27], the algebraic cycles do not appear.

For reductive groups, the cohomology can be computed by lifting to characteristic \(0\): if \(B\) is a Borel subgroup of \(G\), \(G\) is a \(B\)-torsor over \(G/B\); the cohomology of the projective and smooth variety \(G/B\) is invariant under specialization, and one uses the Leray spectral sequence of \(G\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G/B\) to prove the same result for \(G\). It is expressed conveniently in terms of the maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) and of the action of the Weil group \(W\) on \(T\) (for the definition of the maximal torus, cf. [7] or [10]). It is the exterior algebra of its primitive part, which coincides up to a shift with the quotient \(I(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(B G,\mathbb{Q}_\ell))\) of the cohomology of \(B G\) formed of the “indecomposable elements,” and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(B G,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(B T,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)^W\). If \(X\) is the group of characters of \(T\), one has in total
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(G,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) = \bigwedge \left(I\left(\operatorname{Sym}^\bullet(X\otimes \mathbb{Q}_\ell(-1))^W\right)[-1]\right) \text{.} \]

If \(G\) is defined over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{F}_q)\) acts on \(X\) and this isomorphism is compatible with Galois. Passing from there to the cohomology with proper supports, one finds the classical formulas for the number of rational points of \(G\). If \(F^\ast:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is defined by the Frobenius morphism \(F:T\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} T\), and \(\deg_G(F)\) is the degree \(q^{\dim G}\) of \(F:G\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G\), one has
\[ \tag{8.2.1} \left|G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\right| = \deg_G(F) \cdot \det\left(1-{F^\ast}^{-1},I(\operatorname{Sym}^\bullet(X\otimes \mathbb{Q})^W)\right) \text{.} \]

The same formula holds for the Ree and Suzuki groups; these groups are of the form \(G^F\) (\(G\) reductive, \(F^2\) a Frobenius), and it suffices to verify that the Lefschetz trace formula is true for \(F\) acting on \(G\). If \(B\) is a Borel subgroup stable under \(F\), one verifies it directly for \(F\) acting on \(B\), and for the action on \(G/B\), proper and smooth, one may invoke the general theorems.

The trace formula has been used by Deligne-Lusztig [10], Kazhdan [25] and Springer [39] in the study of the complex representations of the finite groups \(G_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\), for \(G_0\) reductive over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). The works of Kazhdan and Springer contain admirable examples of how the trace formula allows the “analytic continuation” of a split situation to a non-split situation (cf. 1.13).
